title: What is Apache Spark?
dek: Start with the problem Spark solves, before the API you write.
idea: Spark is a distributed compute engine. Your data is divided into partitions, and work on those partitions can run in parallel.

sections.title: Why distributed processing?
sections.body:
Imagine computing daily revenue from a year of transaction events. On a laptop, the data may exceed available memory or take longer than your processing window. A distributed engine coordinates work across machines. That coordination has a cost: a small CSV may be simpler and faster to process with pandas or a database.

The useful interview question is: what limits this workload—data size, CPU, I/O, or latency? “Big data” alone is not a sizing decision.

sections.title: Compute is different from storage
sections.body: Spark reads data, computes results, and writes them to a destination. Your source might be object storage or a database; Spark itself is not your permanent database. Storage, table formats, and compute are separate choices.

sections.title: A small example, a useful habit
sections.body: Start with a tiny dataset whose result you can calculate yourself. Here, two successful payments total ₹1,200. The same expression can later operate over partitioned production data. This example assumes a spark session; the next lesson explains its architecture.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
payments = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("success", 500), ("failed", 200), ("success", 700)],
    "status string, amount long"
)
revenue = (payments.filter(F.col("status") == "success")
           .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))
revenue.show()
output: revenue: 1200
pitfall: Spark does not require every dataset to fit in RAM. Distributed processing is also not automatically faster for small workloads.
question: Would you use Spark to process a 20 MB CSV every morning?
answer: First check existing infrastructure, transformations, and latency requirements. A local script or SQL engine may be enough. Spark can still make sense if the pipeline already runs there, but distributed overhead needs a reason.

title: Driver, executors & the cluster
dek: Know who plans the work and who actually runs it.
idea: The driver coordinates your application. Executors run tasks and hold application data. The cluster manager allocates resources.

sections.title: Three roles to keep separate
sections.body: The driver plans and schedules work. The executors are application processes that run tasks. A cluster manager, such as YARN, Kubernetes, or Spark standalone, provides resources. A worker machine is not the same thing as an executor process.

sections.title: Where does your Python run?
sections.body: In classic PySpark, your Python program communicates with Spark’s JVM machinery. Python UDFs can involve Python worker processes on executors. Built-in DataFrame expressions generally execute through Spark’s engine; writing Python syntax does not mean every row runs through Python.

sections.title: Think about the destination
sections.body: A distributed operation can finish successfully and still overwhelm the driver if you bring back too much data. When debugging, inspect a bounded sample and the Spark UI. Ask which process ran out of memory before suggesting more executor memory.

code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("local[2]")  # two local task threads, not two executors
         .appName("spark-fieldnotes")
         .getOrCreate())
spark.range(10).show(5)
output: Shows IDs 0–4, followed by a notice that only five rows are shown.
pitfall: local[2] is a local learning setup, not a two-machine cluster. In production, deployment configuration determines where the driver runs.
question: The driver crashes after collect(), but executors have free memory. Why?
answer: collect() returns all rows to the driver. Diagnose the driver result size and heap rather than only executor capacity. Keep processing distributed, write results to storage, or inspect a bounded sample.

title: RDDs, DataFrames & Spark SQL
dek: Choose the right abstraction for a data engineering pipeline.
idea: For structured ETL, start with DataFrames or SQL: the schema and expressions give Spark information it can optimize.

sections.title: A schema is part of the contract
sections.body: A DataFrame is organized into named, typed columns. Define the expected schema when ingestion needs to be predictable. Check nullability, malformed records, and type conversions explicitly instead of assuming that successful reading means clean data.

sections.title: Where RDDs fit
sections.body: RDDs expose lower-level distributed collections. They are useful for custom processing that does not fit structured expressions. Python DataFrames do not provide the Scala/Java typed Dataset API. In an interview, separate the concepts from language-specific API names.

sections.title: SQL or DataFrame?
sections.body: These are two ways of expressing structured computation through Spark SQL. Choose the form your team can maintain, then inspect the plan. Equivalent logic may produce equivalent plans; switching syntax alone is not a performance strategy.

code:
orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("Pune", 500), ("Delhi", 700), ("Pune", 300)],
    "city string, amount long"
)
orders.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")
spark.sql("""
    SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY city ORDER BY city
""").show()
output: Delhi: 700 · Pune: 800
pitfall: A DataFrame has no guaranteed row order unless you request ordering. Do not rely on the display order of a small test.
question: Is Spark SQL slower than the DataFrame API?
answer: Not inherently. Both use Spark SQL’s engine. Compare the optimized and physical plans for equivalent expressions, plus runtime metrics and UDF use.

title: Lazy evaluation & actions
dek: Understand why a line of code is not a job.
idea: Transformations describe a computation. An action asks Spark to produce a result, triggering the work it needs.

sections.title: Build a plan, then execute
sections.body: Think of a transaction pipeline as a recipe: read, filter, select, aggregate. Describing a recipe is different from cooking it. Deferring execution lets Spark inspect the requested computation before running it.

sections.title: Predict before you run
sections.body: In this example, building even describes a filter. count() asks for a result. A second action can require work again unless an appropriate intermediate result has been persisted and materialized.

sections.title: Use the plan as evidence
sections.body: explain("formatted") helps you inspect execution operators without collecting the dataset. Distinguish planning from execution, and avoid claiming that every API call is free: schema inference and metadata operations can do work too.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
numbers = spark.range(0, 10)
even = numbers.filter(F.col("id") % 2 == 0)
even.explain("formatted")
print(even.count())
output: count() returns 5. The plan contains a range and a filter.
pitfall: Do not say “one action always equals exactly one Spark job.” SQL execution, subqueries, and adaptive execution can make that relationship more involved.
question: I wrote five transformations. How many jobs did I create?
answer: Transformation count alone cannot tell you. Ask which actions run, inspect the executed plan, and confirm in the Spark UI. Lazy transformations primarily build a plan.

title: Jobs, stages & tasks
dek: Read the execution hierarchy without memorizing misleading formulas.
idea: An application runs jobs. Jobs are split into stages, and a stage has tasks that process its partitions.

sections.title: Work at three scales
sections.body: A job is work initiated to obtain a result. A stage groups tasks that can run without crossing a shuffle dependency. Within a stage, tasks operate on partitions. Task attempts can be retried, so attempts and distinct tasks are different counts.

sections.title: Partitions are not CPU cores
sections.body: In the simplified case of 12 ready tasks and four available task slots, execution needs at least three waves. That assumes one slot per task, similar task lengths, and no failures. Twelve partitions do not imply twelve machines.

sections.title: Read the UI from the slow end
sections.body: Find the slow stage, compare task durations, and inspect input sizes and shuffle metrics. One unusually slow task suggests a different investigation from every task being slow. Use evidence to distinguish imbalance from insufficient overall resources.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
events = spark.range(0, 120, 1, 4)
counts = (events.withColumn("bucket", F.col("id") % 3)
          .groupBy("bucket").count())
counts.explain("formatted")
counts.orderBy("bucket").show()
output: Buckets 0, 1, and 2 each have count 40. Exact job/stage counts depend on the executed plan and configuration.
pitfall: A partition is a unit of data; a task is a unit of execution. AQE can change the number of downstream shuffle partitions.
question: You have 200 tasks and 20 available slots. Will the stage take exactly ten task durations?
answer: Ten waves is only a lower-bound model for uniform tasks with no overhead. Skew, scheduling, I/O, retries, and contention affect actual completion time.

title: Partitions & shuffles
dek: Follow the data when work needs to cross partition boundaries.
idea: A shuffle redistributes records across partitions. It is often necessary when records sharing a key must meet.

sections.title: Local work versus redistribution
sections.body: A filter can evaluate rows where they already are. A grouped aggregation needs values for each key brought together. Spark can sometimes reduce data locally first, but the remaining partial results still need appropriate distribution.

sections.title: Repartition or coalesce?
sections.body: repartition redistributes data through a shuffle. coalesce can reduce the partition count without a shuffle, but a drastic reduction can constrain parallelism. Neither operation is a universal fix for output file sizing.

sections.title: Partitioning has several meanings
sections.body: An execution partition is not the same as a storage directory such as date=2026-09-13. Input files, execution partitions, shuffle partitions, and output files are related through execution and writer behavior; they are not interchangeable counts.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
rows = spark.range(0, 12, 1, 3)
keyed = rows.withColumn("key", F.col("id") % 2)
redistributed = keyed.repartition(4, "key")
redistributed.explain("formatted")
output: Look for an Exchange with hash partitioning on key. Four requested partitions do not guarantee four nonempty partitions.
pitfall: More partitions can improve parallelism, but too many tiny tasks add overhead. A hot key can remain hot after repartitioning by that same key.
question: Why did coalesce(1) make my write slow?
answer: It funnels output through one partition and can reduce upstream parallelism. Check file requirements; prefer a useful number of output partitions. A shuffle before the final write trades extra redistribution for parallel upstream work.

title: Joins & data skew
dek: Reason about data shape before reaching for a join hint.
idea: Choose a join strategy using data sizes, key distribution, and the actual execution plan—not table names.

sections.title: Start with correctness
sections.body: Identify the join keys, join type, null behavior, and expected row count. Duplicate keys can multiply output rows. A fast join that changes business grain is still wrong.

sections.title: Small side, large side
sections.body: A broadcast join distributes a build-side relation to executors. It can avoid shuffling the large side for a suitable join, but the broadcast must fit safely. Filter and project the small relation before assessing size. Hints are requests with strategy limitations, not guarantees.

sections.title: When one key dominates
sections.body: If most events share one customer key, hashing that key still sends its records together. Diagnose task and partition imbalance. Possible responses include isolating hot keys, pre-aggregation where valid, or carefully designed salting. Check correctness when combining salted results.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
facts = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 100), (2, 200)],
                              "customer_id long, amount long")
customers = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Pune"), (2, "Delhi")],
                                  "customer_id long, city string")
joined = facts.join(F.broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
joined.explain("formatted")
joined.orderBy("customer_id").show()
output: Two matching rows: customer 1 / 100 / Pune and customer 2 / 200 / Delhi.
pitfall: Do not broadcast a relation simply because it is smaller than the other table. Its expanded size and executor memory pressure matter.
question: A join finishes 199 tasks quickly and one task takes 20 minutes. What do you inspect?
answer: Compare the slow task’s input and shuffle size, spill, and execution time. Check hot or null keys and join multiplicity. Consider adaptive skew handling where applicable; do not assume that adding executors splits a single hot partition.

title: Caching & fault tolerance
dek: Reuse the right work, and know what Spark can recompute.
idea: Caching is a reuse decision. Recovery relies on the ability to recompute missing work from available inputs.

sections.title: Cache a reusable boundary
sections.body: If several actions reuse an expensive filtered dataset, persisting that intermediate result may help. Materialization costs time and storage. Compare total runtime, check the Storage tab, and release data when its reuse window ends.

sections.title: Be precise about defaults
sections.body: In PySpark 3.5.7, DataFrame cache() uses MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER. Do not transfer this default to every RDD API or version. Storage settings and eviction determine what remains available for reuse.

sections.title: Recovery has boundaries
sections.body: Spark can recompute lost RDD partitions using lineage. That requires usable upstream inputs; it does not promise that every external side effect runs exactly once. Retry-aware writes, deterministic logic, and appropriate transactional sinks are separate design decisions.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
reusable = spark.range(100).filter(F.col("id") % 2 == 0).cache()
try:
    print(reusable.count())  # materializes this small example
    reusable.agg(F.sum("id").alias("total")).show()
finally:
    reusable.unpersist()
output: count: 50 · total: 2450
pitfall: Calling cache() alone does not eagerly materialize the dataset. Cached data can also be evicted or lost.
question: Is caching every DataFrame a good way to speed up my pipeline?
answer: No. Identify repeated expensive computation, memory capacity, and reuse lifetime. Caching one-use intermediates can add overhead and pressure. Measure, inspect storage, and unpersist deliberately.

title: Executor memory, spill & out-of-memory errors
dek: Understand where an executor's memory goes, why Spark spills to disk, and how to read an out-of-memory failure.
idea: Execution and storage share one bounded memory region. Spill is the graceful fallback when execution outgrows it; an out-of-memory error is what happens when a single unit of work — a task's partition, a collect(), or one hot key — cannot fit even with spilling.

sections.title: Where the memory goes
sections.body:
An executor is a JVM process plus whatever runs beside it. spark.executor.memory sizes the JVM heap. spark.executor.memoryOverhead budgets additional memory for VM overheads, native allocations, and Python workers when spark.executor.pyspark.memory is unset. If overhead is not set explicitly, Spark uses spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor with a 384 MiB minimum: the factor defaults to 0.10, except for Kubernetes non-JVM jobs such as PySpark, where it defaults to 0.40.

On YARN and Kubernetes, the executor container budget is the sum of spark.executor.memory, spark.executor.memoryOverhead, enabled off-heap memory (spark.memory.offHeap.size), and separately configured spark.executor.pyspark.memory. The optional allocations add to the container request; Python workers share the overhead budget when no separate PySpark allocation is configured.

Inside the heap, Spark reserves 300 MiB for system use, then splits what remains. spark.memory.fraction (default 0.6) is the region shared by execution and storage memory; spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5) marks how much of that region cached blocks can claim without being evicted.

  • Execution memory holds working state: shuffle buffers, sort runs, and hash tables for joins and aggregations.
  • Storage memory holds cached blocks for reuse.
  • Execution may evict cached storage when it needs space. Storage may never evict execution — the source comments call this out as a deliberate simplification.

Two consequences matter in interviews: a pandas conversion or a large broadcast lands somewhere specific — driver or executor — and a cache that seems to disappear under heavy compute is the eviction rule at work, not a bug.

Check the sources: Executor memory configuration · Memory tuning overview · UnifiedMemoryManager

sections.title: What spills, and what it costs
sections.body:
Operators that need to see many rows at once — sorts, hash aggregations, shuffle writers — accumulate state in execution memory. When the memory manager cannot grant more, spillable structures write sorted runs to local disk and merge them later. The sort path carries an explicit element threshold that forces a spill before the structure grows arbitrarily, and spilled files land in Spark's configured local scratch directories, not remote storage.

Spill is graceful, not fatal: the stage completes more slowly because it traded memory pressure for disk I/O. It deserves action when it is large relative to the stage's input, or when it concentrates in a few tasks — compare tasks with each other instead of expecting any fixed size.

The Spark UI reports it directly. The Stages tab lists Shuffle spill (memory) — the deserialized form of the shuffled data held in memory — and Shuffle spill (disk) — the serialized form written to disk — next to peak execution memory and GC time. The SQL tab attributes spill size and peak memory to specific operators such as Sort and HashAggregate.

Check the sources: Web UI metrics · UnsafeExternalSorter

sections.title: Three out-of-memory failures, three places to look
sections.body:
Driver OOM. The driver collects or materializes too much: collect(), toPandas(), a huge returned result, or a giant broadcast. spark.driver.maxResultSize exists to abort a job before this happens; the limit lives in the driver's heap, not an executor's.

Executor task OOM. The working set of one task is too large — one oversized partition, or one hot key carrying a disproportionate share of rows. This is the failure the tuning guide describes for reduce-side operations, and its first suggested fix is more parallelism, so each task's input set is smaller. Adding executors does not split the offending partition.

Container or overhead kill. The process is killed by YARN or Kubernetes for exceeding the container's memory limit while the JVM heap looks healthy. What ran out is non-heap memory: overhead, off-heap allocations, or a PySpark worker — Python memory lives outside the JVM heap and counts against overhead unless spark.executor.pyspark.memory sets its own limit.

Read the failure location, not just the exception text: driver logs, executor stderr, exit codes, and the Spark UI's per-task view each point at a different one of these.

Check the sources: Configuration reference · Memory tuning overview

sections.title: How to debug it, in order
sections.body:
Work from observation to action, and keep the unit of work in mind at every step:

  1. Locate the failure. Driver log, executor stderr, or a killed container. Find the stage and the tasks that failed or slowed first.
  2. Classify the pressure. Spill and GC high across every task suggests general memory pressure; one task far above the median suggests skew or an oversized partition.
  3. Shrink the unit of work. More or smaller partitions make each task's working set smaller; avoid collecting results to the driver, and fix skew where the data shape allows it.
  4. Check memory hygiene. Unpersist what is no longer reused — caching everything competes with execution memory.
  5. Only then change memory sizes. Raise executor memory when the single unit genuinely needs it; raise overhead when containers were killed despite a healthy heap; treat Python worker memory separately for PySpark.

Interviewers listen for exactly this structure: where the failure happened, which unit could not fit, and why the chosen fix changes that unit's size — instead of "add more executors" applied blindly.

Check the sources: Memory tuning overview · Configuration reference

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = spark.read.parquet("orders")  # customer_id, amount

totals = (
    orders
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
)

totals.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("customer_totals")
output: One row per distinct customer_id. Whether this stage spills depends on data size, partitioning, and executor memory — read the stage's Shuffle Spill (memory) and (disk) columns in the Spark UI rather than expecting a fixed amount.
pitfall: Reading "OutOfMemoryError" as "add more executors". Executor count cannot split a single oversized partition, one collect() result, or one hot key. Find which unit of work failed to fit first.
question: A groupBy job fails with OutOfMemoryError. How do you decide whether to change the data layout, the code, or the executor configuration?
answer: Locate the failure before changing anything: a driver OOM points at collect-style code or oversized driver structures; a task OOM in a few tasks points at skew or oversized partitions; a container kill with a healthy heap points at overhead or Python worker memory. From there: fix skew or partition size to shrink the largest unit of work, stop materializing results on the driver, and review caching so storage is not competing with execution. Change memory sizes last, and only for the component that actually died — adding executors rarely fixes a single unit that cannot fit, because one task still processes one partition.

title: Reading the Spark UI and fixing slow jobs
dek: Start from the slowest stage, compare tasks, then read the SQL plan before changing anything.
idea: The UI separates what ran (jobs and stages) from what it cost (task distribution) and why (SQL operators). Diagnose in that order, and fix data layout before configuration.

sections.title: Start from the slow end
sections.body:
Open the Jobs tab first: it lists every job with status, duration, and a tasks progress bar, plus an event timeline of executors and jobs. Click the longest-running job to reach its detail page — event timeline, DAG visualization, and its stages grouped by state (active, pending, completed, skipped, failed).

From there, open the Stages tab and sort by duration. Each stage row shows how far its tasks progressed, how much it read from storage, and how much it shuffled: shuffle read (bytes and records read, local plus remote) and shuffle write (bytes and records written for a later stage to read). The slowest stage is your investigation target — not the first stage, and not an average over the whole application.

Two checks before drilling in: the Executors tab tells you whether executors were even available (memory, cores, task and shuffle counts, GC time), and the Environment tab shows explicitly supplied SparkContext properties, including startup memory settings; default values are not all listed. Session SQL changes made with spark.conf.set(...) or SQL SET are not reflected there. Before running the query, read the current session values with spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions") and spark.conf.get("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled"), or SQL SET, then inspect the executed plan. Debugging a slow job with the wrong assumed config wastes the whole pass.

Check the sources: Web UI: Jobs, Stages, Executors, Environment tabs · Startup properties and runtime SQL configuration

sections.title: Jobs, stages, and the task distribution
sections.body:
A job is a triggered computation; a stage is the set of tasks that can run without redistributing data; a task is one partition processed in one attempt. The stage detail page makes this concrete: total time across all tasks, locality-level summary, shuffle read size and records, associated job IDs, and a DAG whose nodes are grouped by operation scope (BatchScan, WholeStageCodegen, Exchange).

Read the summary metrics table, not just the duration: task duration, GC time, result serialization and result-fetch time, scheduler delay, peak execution memory, shuffle read size and records, shuffle fetch wait time (tasks blocked waiting on remote shuffle data), remote reads, shuffle write time, and shuffle spill (memory) versus (disk) — the deserialized bytes held in memory and the serialized bytes written to disk. The same metrics aggregated by executor show whether one executor carried the load; the per-task table shows duration, input, shuffle, spill, and GC per task, with logs and attempt numbers for failures.

  • Every task slow together suggests general pressure: too little parallelism, oversized partitions, heavy spill and GC everywhere, or data fetched from far away (compare PROCESS_LOCAL and NODE_LOCAL against RACK_LOCAL and ANY).
  • One task far above the median suggests skew or one oversized partition: compare its input and shuffle size, spill, and duration against the median task instead of trusting the stage average.

The tuning guide's first fix for an oversized reduce-side working set is more parallelism so each task's input set is smaller — Spark reuses one executor JVM across many tasks and supports tasks as short as 200 ms. Recommend 2–3 tasks per CPU core as a starting point, not a guarantee.

Check the sources: Web UI: stage and task metrics · Tuning: parallelism, reduce memory, locality

sections.title: Read the SQL plan with the stages
sections.body:
The SQL tab lists each executed query with duration, associated jobs, and its physical and logical plans. Its detail page shows the query DAG — WholeStageCodegen blocks (with codegen IDs such as WholeStageCodegen (1)) fusing scans, filters, and partial aggregates into one function, and Exchange blocks carrying shuffle metrics such as records written and data size. A Details link exposes the parsed, analyzed, optimized, and physical plans; operators subject to whole-stage codegen are prefixed with a star and codegen ID.

Each operator block reports SQL metrics: number of output rows after a filter, aggregate, or join; shuffle bytes written and write time on an Exchange; spill size and peak memory on Sort and HashAggregate; scan and metadata time on file scans; build-side size and hash-map build time on joins. Use these to name the expensive operator: a Sort with large spill size is an execution-memory problem; an Exchange with huge remote reads plus high fetch wait is a redistribution problem; a join whose build side dwarfs the threshold is a strategy problem.

Cross-reference both directions: stage DAG nodes carry scope names and codegen IDs that map back to the SQL plan, and the SQL page links each query to its jobs. The Storage tab completes the picture for reuse — persisted DataFrames appear only after an action materializes them, with storage level, size, and partition counts. A cache that never appears was never materialized; a cache that shrinks under compute lost to execution eviction.

Check the sources: Web UI: SQL metrics and Storage tab

sections.title: Fix in order: layout, code, then config
sections.body:
Work from observation to the smallest change that shrinks the largest unit of work:

  1. Shrink or rebalance the unit of work. More or smaller partitions for oversized reduce inputs; avoid collect() and toPandas() on large results; fix hot or null keys where the data shape allows it. Adding executors does not split one hot partition.
  2. Check reuse hygiene. Cache only repeatedly read inputs, confirm materialization in the Storage tab, and unpersist what is no longer reused — cached blocks compete with execution memory.
  3. Let the optimizer help where eligible. Adaptive query execution is enabled by default since Spark 3.2 under spark.sql.adaptive.enabled: it coalesces post-shuffle partitions from a large initial count, converts sort-merge joins to broadcast joins when a side proves small at runtime, and splits skewed sort-merge join partitions. Each has eligibility and threshold requirements — read the executed plan rather than assuming AQE removed the shuffle.
  4. Change configuration last, for the component that died. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions for shuffle parallelism, AQE size thresholds for coalescing and skew handling, broadcast thresholds for join strategy, memory settings for genuine capacity shortfalls. Confirm startup Spark properties in the Environment tab. For session SQL changes, use spark.conf.get(...) or SQL SET in the session that will run the query. Re-run it and inspect the executed plan and stage metrics to verify the effect.

Interviewers listen for this sequence: slowest stage first, task distribution second, SQL operator third, fix last — with the UI screen named at each step instead of "tune Spark" applied blindly.

Check the sources: SQL tuning: shuffle partitions and AQE · Tuning: parallelism and reduce memory · Startup properties and runtime SQL configuration

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = spark.read.parquet("orders")  # order_id, customer_id, amount

totals = (
    orders
    .repartition(200, "customer_id")
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
)

totals.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("customer_totals")
output: One row per distinct customer_id. Which stage is slowest, how task durations spread, and whether the Exchange or HashAggregate carries spill depends on data size and partitioning — read the Jobs, Stages, and SQL tabs rather than expecting fixed counts.
pitfall: Reading the stage average instead of the task distribution. An average hides the one straggler task that defines the stage's finish time — compare the slowest tasks against the median, then name the operator.
question: A stage has 199 fast tasks and one task that takes 20 minutes. Where do you look first, and what do you change last?
answer: Start from the slow end: Jobs tab to the longest job, Stages tab to the longest stage, then the per-task table comparing the straggler's input, shuffle read, spill, and duration against the median. Cross to the SQL tab to name the operator holding that data — Exchange, Sort, or HashAggregate with its spill size and peak memory. Fix data layout first (partitioning, hot or null keys, driver-side collection), check cache hygiene, consider eligible AQE skew handling, and change configuration last for the component that actually failed.

title: Catalyst, code generation & AQE
dek: Follow a DataFrame from parsed plan to executed plan, read what explain prints, and see what adaptive execution changes once real sizes arrive.
idea: Catalyst rewrites the logical plan with rules, then plans it physically by applying strategies in a fixed order to size estimates — it does not cost-compare physical plans. Adaptive query execution re-plans the rest of a query each time a shuffle stage finishes, using measured sizes instead of estimates.

sections.title: From DataFrame to executed plan
sections.body:
A DataFrame is a description of work. Its QueryExecution turns that description into something that runs, in a fixed sequence, and explain("extended") prints each stage:

  1. Parsed logical plan — the tree as written, still unresolved. For the example below it begins 'Aggregate ['category], ['category, sum('gross) AS total#12]; the leading quote marks names not yet resolved.
  2. Analyzed logical plan — names resolved against the schema and catalog, types checked, and every attribute given an ID such as amount#2. Analysis runs as soon as you build the DataFrame: selecting a misspelled column raised AnalysisException before any action.
  3. Optimized logical plan — batches of rewrite rules. The filter amount > 10 became isnotnull(amount#2) AND (amount#2 > 10.0): a null check was inferred and the analyzer's cast(10 as double) folded into a literal.
  4. Physical plan — operators that execute: Scan, Filter, Project, a partial and a final HashAggregate, and the Exchange between them. What explain prints here is the prepared plan, after exchanges and code generation stages were added.

Read physical plans bottom up: data flows from the scan toward the root. The other modes answer other questions. "formatted" prints a numbered outline followed by per-operator details — Input, Condition, Keys, Functions, and for file scans PartitionFilters and PushedFilters — which is easier to scan than one long tree. "cost" prints the optimized logical plan with its statistics when they are available, and "codegen" prints generated code when there is any.

Check the sources: EXPLAIN modes · DataFrame.explain · QueryExecution source

sections.title: Physical planning: rule order, estimates, and where cost enters
sections.body:
SparkPlanner holds a list of strategies — join selection, aggregation, file-source scans, basic operators — and applies them to the optimized plan. The planner interface can yield several candidates, but in Spark 3.5.7 QueryExecution.createSparkPlan takes the first one: its source comment says it uses next() "for now, but we will implement to choose the best plan." No search costs alternative physical plans against each other.

Choices such as the join strategy are rules evaluated in order. For an equi-join, JoinSelection checks hints first. Without an applicable hint it picks a broadcast hash join if one side's estimated size fits spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB) and the join type allows it; then a shuffled hash join only if one side is small enough for a local hash map, much smaller than the other, and spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin is false; then a sort-merge join for sortable keys; and finally a cartesian product or broadcast nested loop join.

Cost enters through statistics on the logical plan. By default Spark estimates size only: a file relation reports its file size, and a filter keeps its child's estimate. A 1,000-row table filtered to amount > 900 still estimated 5.5 KiB. ANALYZE TABLE … COMPUTE STATISTICS records size and row count for a catalog table, and FOR COLUMNS adds column statistics such as min, max, null count, and distinct count. Those numbers drive estimates only when spark.sql.cbo.enabled is true, and it is false by default. With column statistics and CBO on, the same filter estimated rowCount=100 and 2000 B; with CBO off, the estimate stayed 5.5 KiB. Cost-based join reordering also requires spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.enabled, false by default.

The accurate summary: rule-based logical optimization and rule-ordered physical planning, fed by estimates that become cost-based only when you collect statistics and turn CBO on. Better estimates change the physical plan by changing what the rules see.

sections.title: Preparations: exchanges and whole-stage codegen
sections.body:
The chosen physical plan still needs preparation rules. In 3.5.7 they include PlanSubqueries, RemoveRedundantProjects, EnsureRequirements, RemoveRedundantSorts, ApplyColumnarRulesAndInsertTransitions, CollapseCodegenStages, and exchange reuse. With AQE enabled, InsertAdaptiveSparkPlan runs first; when it wraps the query in AdaptiveSparkPlan, the remaining rules are applied later, stage by stage, as the adaptive plan executes.

EnsureRequirements compares what each operator needs from its children — a hash distribution on the grouping keys, a sort order for a sort-merge join — with what they produce, and inserts a shuffle Exchange or a Sort where they differ. That is the origin of Exchange hashpartitioning(category#1, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS between the partial and final aggregates.

CollapseCodegenStages fuses each run of adjacent operators that support code generation into one generated Java function. A *(n) prefix marks membership in codegen stage n. The run breaks at an operator without codegen support, and at one whose expressions need the interpreted fallback. Observed boundaries:

  • Exchange separated *(1) (scan, filter, project, partial aggregate) from *(2) (final aggregate).
  • collect_list planned as ObjectHashAggregate, printed without a star.
  • A Python UDF became BatchEvalPython, splitting *(1) below from *(2) above — inside one scheduler stage, since no shuffle was involved. A codegen stage ID is not a scheduler stage ID.
  • A Project computing transform(xs, x -> x * 2) lost its star: that higher-order function evaluates through the interpreted fallback, although it never leaves the JVM.

Codegen can also switch itself off: if a generated method's bytecode exceeds the internal spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit (65535), whole-stage codegen is deactivated for that subtree.

With AQE on, look after execution. Before an action, AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false showed no *(n) markers, and explain("codegen") reported "Found 0 WholeStageCodegen subtrees." After collect(), the final plan showed *(1) and *(2). With AQE disabled, the same query showed both stages up front and found 2 subtrees.

Check the sources: Preparation rules · EnsureRequirements · WholeStageCodegenExec · AdaptiveSparkPlanExec

sections.title: What blocks predicate pushdown
sections.body:
A file scan in the physical plan lists three kinds of filter. PartitionFilters are evaluated by Spark against partition values from the directory listing, so pruned directories are never opened. PushedFilters are predicates translated into the data source filter API and handed to the reader; for Parquet, that lets the reader skip data using its statistics. DataFilters are the data-column predicates. Spark keeps a Filter above the scan for every non-partition predicate, so pushdown saves reading, not correctness checks.

Translation accepts specific shapes: a column compared with a literal, IN with literals, null checks, string prefix, suffix, and contains tests, and AND/OR/NOT combinations of those. Everything else stays in Spark. On a 3,000-row Parquet dataset partitioned by day (3 directories, 6 files):

Filters the scan received for each predicate (local PySpark 3.5.7)
PredicateWhat the scan receivedWhy
amount > 400PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,400)]A column compared with a literal translates into a source filter.
The same test in a Python UDFPushedFilters: []; Filter above BatchEvalPythonThe UDF moves into its own operator; the reader sees no predicate.
cast(amount as string) = '450'Only IsNotNull(amount)A function around the column has no source-filter equivalent.
amount > 400 AND rand(7) < 0.5GreaterThan(amount,400) pushed; rand stays in SparkNon-deterministic expressions are not pushed; deterministic conjuncts still are.
user_id < 10 OR amount > 400Or(LessThan(user_id,10),GreaterThan(amount,400))An OR of translatable predicates translates.
day = '2026-09-02' (partition column)PartitionFilters; 2 of 6 files readDirectories that cannot match are never opened.
cast(day as string) = '2026-09-02'Still PartitionFilters; 2 of 6 files readSpark evaluates deterministic partition-only predicates itself.
Python UDF on dayNo partition or pushed filter; 6 of 6 files readA Python UDF cannot run during partition pruning.
day = '2026-09-02' OR amount > 400Neither; 6 of 6 files readThe OR mixes a directory value with a file column, so it is neither prunable nor pushable.

Pushdown depends on the shape of an expression, not on how simple it looks. Write predicates as built-in expressions, compare columns to literals rather than wrapping the column, and keep partition predicates separate from data predicates. Then confirm in the plan and in the scan's files-read metric. Storage formats explains what a Parquet reader does with a pushed filter; Lazy evaluation shows why the plan exists before anything is read.

sections.title: Adaptive query execution: re-planning between stages
sections.body:
AQE is enabled by default since Spark 3.2.0 (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled). AdaptiveSparkPlanExec splits the plan into query stages at exchanges, runs the stages whose inputs are ready, and after each stage materializes it re-optimizes and re-plans the rest of the query using the measured output. It wraps queries that contain an exchange or a subquery, or whose operators require a distribution; a plain filtered scan is not wrapped.

Before an action, explain prints AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false. After an action, explain on the same DataFrame prints isFinalPlan=true with a == Final Plan == and the == Initial Plan ==. The final plan names completed stages (ShuffleQueryStage 0, BroadcastQueryStage 2) and how their output is read: AQEShuffleRead coalesced, local, or skewed. The SQL tab in the Spark UI shows the same final plan.

  • Coalescing post-shuffle partitions. A groupBy over 10 keys with the default 200 shuffle partitions ran its reduce stage as 1 task behind AQEShuffleRead coalesced; with coalescing disabled, the same stage ran 200 tasks. Under the default spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.parallelismFirst=true, Spark ignores the 64 MB advisory size and respects only the 1 MB minimum partition size; the setting's own description recommends false.
  • Switching a join to broadcast. A Parquet side filtered to 50 rows kept its 13.4 MiB file-size estimate, so under a 1 MiB broadcast threshold the initial plan was SortMergeJoin. After both shuffle map stages ran, the final plan was BroadcastHashJoin, reading each shuffle through AQEShuffleRead local. The shuffle writes had already happened; the switch saved the sorts and reduce-side fetches. (The optimizer had also inferred fk < 50 for the other side from the join key, so that side was built.) Converting to a shuffled hash join instead requires spark.sql.adaptive.maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold above its default of 0.
  • Splitting skewed partitions. A join partition counts as skewed when it exceeds both 5 × the median partition size and 256 MB (defaults). With both thresholds lowered for a laptop-sized dataset, the plan showed SortMergeJoin(skew=true) and AQEShuffleRead skewed, and the join stage ran 9 tasks instead of 8. The documentation describes sort-merge joins; the 3.5.7 rule also matches shuffled hash joins.

Check the sources: AQE guide · AdaptiveSparkPlanExec · InsertAdaptiveSparkPlan · OptimizeSkewedJoin · AQE settings

sections.title: What AQE cannot fix
sections.body:
AQE changes decisions that come after a completed stage, using that stage's output sizes. That leaves a lot out of reach:

  • Work already done. A runtime broadcast arrives after the shuffle map stages were written. If you know a side is small, let the static plan broadcast it: collect statistics or add a hint you have checked.
  • The first read. Scan parallelism comes from file splitting (spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes), not from AQE. Thousands of small files, an unpushable predicate, or unsorted data that defeats row-group statistics are untouched.
  • Queries without an exchange. They are not wrapped in an adaptive plan at all.
  • Hot keys outside joins. Skew splitting covers joins and rebalance partitions. One huge key in a groupBy or a window still lands in one task, and coalescing only merges partitions — it never splits one.
  • Opaque code. A Python UDF still blocks pushdown of predicates on its result and splits codegen.
  • Memory inside one task or the driver. A partition too large for its task, or a large collect(), is not a planning decision.

Treat the final plan as evidence of what AQE decided, then fix the remaining cause where it lives: file layout, the query's expressions, or configuration. Joins & data skew covers manual fixes when AQE's split is not enough.

Check the sources: AQE guide · When AQE applies · OptimizeSkewedJoin

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "books", 12.0), (2, "games", 30.0), (3, "books", 8.0), (4, "music", 15.0)],
    "order_id INT, category STRING, amount DOUBLE",
)

totals = (
    orders.filter(F.col("amount") > 10)
    .select("category", (F.col("amount") * 1.1).alias("gross"))
    .groupBy("category")
    .agg(F.sum("gross").alias("total"))
)

totals.explain("extended")  # parsed, analyzed, optimized, physical
totals.collect()            # run it: AQE plans each stage with real sizes
totals.explain()            # same DataFrame: now the final and initial plans
output: The extended explain printed four plans. The optimized plan's filter read isnotnull(amount#2) AND (amount#2 > 10.0). The physical plan was AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false with Exchange hashpartitioning(category#1, 200) between a partial and a final HashAggregate, and no *(n) codegen markers. After collect(), explain() on the same DataFrame printed isFinalPlan=true: a Final Plan with *(1) around the scan, filter, project, and partial aggregate, then ShuffleQueryStage 0, AQEShuffleRead coalesced, and *(2) around the final aggregate, followed by the Initial Plan. Attribute and plan IDs vary between runs; whether and how far partitions coalesce depends on data size and the spark.sql.adaptive settings.
runtime: Ran on local PySpark 3.5.7 (local[2], JDK 17) with default SQL settings on 2026-09-15; output above is observed.
pitfall: Reading the pre-execution explain as the plan that ran. With AQE on, the initial plan can show a sort-merge join that became a broadcast join, 200 shuffle partitions that became one task, and no codegen markers at all. Run the action, then read the final plan — from explain on the same DataFrame or in the SQL tab — and remember that a plan produced from a small local sample can differ from the one production sizes produce.
question: An explain before an action shows a sort-merge join and 200 shuffle partitions, but the SQL tab shows a broadcast hash join and far fewer tasks. Which plan is wrong?
answer: Neither. With AQE enabled, explain before an action prints the initial adaptive plan, built from static estimates: a filtered file relation keeps its file-size estimate, so the join side exceeded the broadcast threshold, and the shuffle used the configured partition count. At run time each shuffle map stage reported its real output size. AQE re-planned the rest of the query, switched to a broadcast hash join once a side proved small, and coalesced the small post-shuffle partitions. The SQL tab, and explain on the same DataFrame after the action, show the final plan with the initial plan kept for comparison. The shuffle writes before the switch still happened.

title: PySpark UDFs, Arrow & the Python boundary
dek: See where your Python function actually runs, what crosses into it, and why the fastest UDF is usually the one you did not need to write.
idea: A Python UDF runs in separate Python worker processes, so data must be serialized out of the JVM and back, and Catalyst treats the function as a black box. Arrow changes how data crosses that boundary; only a pandas UDF also changes how your function processes it.

sections.title: Where Python runs
sections.body:
Your PySpark program runs in a Python process on the driver, but DataFrame calls — filter, groupBy, even F.upper — only build a plan that the JVM executes (see RDDs, DataFrames & Spark SQL). When built-in expressions run on executors, no Python is involved.

A Python UDF is different: its function must run in Python beside the data. Executors hand that work to Python worker processes, reused across tasks by default (spark.python.worker.reuse=true). In a local run, a UDF returning os.getpid() reported worker PIDs 31531 and 31532, while the driver's Python PID was 31455 — the function never ran in the driver's interpreter.

For an ordinary Python UDF, the BatchEvalPython operator projects the UDF's input columns, groups rows into batches, pickles them, and writes them over a socket to the worker. The worker unpickles each batch, calls your function once per row, pickles the results, and sends them back. The JVM unpickles each result and pairs it with the original row, which it held in a queue meanwhile. Every row pays for conversion into Python objects and back, plus a Python function call.

Check the sources: EvalPythonExec · BatchEvalPythonExec · Python worker settings

sections.title: Why the optimizer stops at a UDF
sections.body:
Catalyst cannot read Python code, so a UDF is an opaque expression with a declared return type. ExtractPythonUDFs moves Python UDFs out of projections and filters into dedicated operators, and the plan makes the boundary visible. Upper-casing a name column four ways, followed by filter(id > 1):

Physical plans observed on local PySpark 3.5.7
ImplementationOperator in the planWhole-stage codegen
F.upper("name")Project with upper(name#1)One stage: *(1) project, filter, scan
@udfBatchEvalPython [upper_py(name#1)]*(1) below, *(2) above
@udf(useArrow=True)ArrowEvalPython [...], 101*(1) below, *(2) above
@pandas_udf (Series to Series)ArrowEvalPython [...], 200*(1) below, *(2) above

The trailing number is the Python evaluation type: 101 is an Arrow-batched Python UDF and 200 a scalar pandas UDF. Two consequences follow.

  • Codegen splits around the Python operator; operators below and above still generate code, in separate stages.
  • Predicates on the UDF's result cannot be pushed. On a Parquet dataset, filter(amount > 400) pushed GreaterThan(amount,400) into the scan; the same test written as a Python UDF left PushedFilters: [] and a Filter above BatchEvalPython, so every row was read first. Both returned 594 rows. Predicates that do not touch the UDF still move below it: id > 1 ran before the UDF in all four plans.

Spark treats a UDF as deterministic unless you call asNondeterministic(), and the API notes warn that it may be invoked more or fewer times than it appears in the query. Selecting a UDF result and then filtering on that column pushed the filter below the projection by copying the expression, so the plan evaluated the UDF in two BatchEvalPython operators; marked non-deterministic, it was evaluated once. See Catalyst, code generation & AQE for how to read these plans.

Check the sources: ExtractPythonUDFs · Python eval types · udf notes

sections.title: Arrow: batches across the boundary, pandas inside it
sections.body:
Apache Arrow is a columnar in-memory format. Spark uses it to move column batches between the JVM and Python instead of pickled rows. What your function receives depends on the API:

  • Arrow-optimized Python UDF — @udf(..., useArrow=True), or for every eligible UDF spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled (default false; the setting dates from Spark 3.4.0). Transfer uses Arrow, but the function is still called row by row: the 3.5.7 worker loops over each batch and calls it per row, and the guide calls these UDFs "executed row-by-row." Arrow's return-type coercion can differ from the pickled path, which the source gives as the reason the option is off by default.
  • pandas UDF — @pandas_udf with Python type hints. Series to Series (output length must equal input); Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series, useful when execution needs expensive state initialized once; Iterator of multiple Series; and Series to scalar, an aggregate for groupBy().agg() or unbounded windows that loads each group into memory with no partial aggregation (planned as AggregateInPandas after an Exchange and Sort). The function receives whole batches, so vectorized pandas or NumPy code avoids a Python call per row. Type hints are preferred; the guide says PandasUDFType will be deprecated.
  • pandas function APIs take and return pandas DataFrames. mapInPandas maps an iterator of DataFrames per partition and may return any number of rows; it planned as MapInPandas over the scan, with no shuffle. groupBy().applyInPandas hands each group to your function as one DataFrame and requires a full shuffle: Exchange, Sort, FlatMapGroupsInPandas. cogroup().applyInPandas does the same for two grouped DataFrames.

Batch size. spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch (default 10,000) caps rows per Arrow batch. A pandas UDF over one 25,000-row partition saw batches of 10,000, 10,000, and 5,000 rows; at 1,000, every batch had 1,000 rows. The cap counts rows, not bytes, so wide rows may need a lower value. It does not apply to applyInPandas or cogroup: each whole group is one batch, and a skewed group can exhaust the worker.

Check the sources: Arrow and pandas guide · worker.py · pandas_udf · mapInPandas · applyInPandas

sections.title: Memory for Python workers
sections.body:
Python workers are native processes outside the executor's JVM heap, so spark.executor.memory does not size them. By default spark.executor.pyspark.memory is unset: Spark does not limit Python's memory, and Python workers share spark.executor.memoryOverhead with other non-JVM memory in the container. On YARN and Kubernetes, a container that exceeds its total can be killed while the heap looks healthy.

Setting spark.executor.pyspark.memory does two things. On YARN and Kubernetes it adds that amount to the executor's resource request. And PythonRunner divides it by the executor's cores and passes the result to each worker, which applies it as an address-space limit through Python's resource module. The configuration reference notes that the limit is not supported on Windows and not enforced on macOS, so it cannot be tested on a Mac laptop.

Two neighbors are easy to confuse. spark.python.worker.memory (512m) only sets when a Python worker spills to disk during aggregation. And Arrow batches take JVM memory while they are built — the guide warns this "can temporarily lead to high memory usage in the JVM." toPandas() collects the whole result to the driver whether or not Arrow is enabled. Executor memory explains how the container total adds up.

Check the sources: PySpark memory settings · PythonRunner · worker.py limits · Arrow batch memory · toPandas

sections.title: Choose the least opaque tool
sections.body:
1. Built-in functions and SQL expressions. Catalyst can optimize them, push eligible predicates, and generate code. Check the built-in list first — string, date, JSON, regex, and conditional logic are mostly covered.
  2. Higher-order functions such as transform, filter, exists, and aggregate for array and map columns. They stay in the JVM with no Python round trip, although in the observed plan the Project using transform fell out of whole-stage codegen.
  3. pandas UDFs or pandas function APIs when the logic genuinely needs Python libraries, written with vectorized operations. Series.apply inside a pandas UDF is still a Python call per row.
  4. A row-at-a-time Python UDF as the last resort. Consider useArrow=True after checking that its type coercion gives the results you expect.

An illustration, not a benchmark. On one laptop (local[2], 2,000,000 cached strings, best of three runs of summing the length of upper-cased values), the built-in took 0.15 s, the pandas UDF 0.38 s, the Arrow Python UDF 0.60 s, and the plain Python UDF 1.22 s. Those ratios come from one trivial function on one machine. The gap changes with the function's own cost, data types, batch size, row width, and cluster layout, so there is no general "10–100×" multiplier. Compare plans first, then time a representative sample of your own job.

Check the sources: Built-in functions · Arrow and pandas guide · udf

output: The built-in plan was a single codegen stage: *(1) Project [id#0, upper(name#1) AS u#7] over *(1) Filter (isnotnull(id#0) AND (id#0 > 1)) and the scan. The Python UDF plan inserted BatchEvalPython [upper_py(name#1)#4] between *(1) Filter/Scan and *(2) Project. The Arrow Python UDF and the pandas UDF both inserted ArrowEvalPython, with eval types 101 and 200. In every plan the id > 1 filter ran below the UDF. Requires pandas and PyArrow installed; attribute IDs vary between runs.

pitfall: Assuming useArrow=True or a pandas UDF makes Python code fast by itself. Arrow changes how batches cross the boundary: an Arrow Python UDF still calls your function once per row, and a pandas UDF whose body uses Series.apply or a Python loop is still per-row Python. Neither lets Catalyst push a predicate through the function or fuse it into generated code. Check the plan for BatchEvalPython or ArrowEvalPython, and time a representative sample before and after the change.
question: A teammate wraps a string cleanup in @udf, finds it slow, and adds useArrow=True. What changed, and what did not?
answer: The transfer changed: rows now reach the Python worker as Arrow batches instead of pickled rows, and the plan shows ArrowEvalPython instead of BatchEvalPython. In Spark 3.5.7 the worker still calls the function once per row, so the per-row Python call remains, and Arrow's return-type coercion can differ from the pickled path, which needs checking. What did not change: the function is still opaque, so a predicate on its result cannot be pushed into the scan and whole-stage codegen still splits around it. If the cleanup exists as built-in functions such as trim, lower, or regexp_replace, use those; if it truly needs Python, move to a pandas UDF with a vectorized body. Confirm with the plan and a timed sample.

title: Storage formats: Parquet, ORC & Avro
dek: Why the file layout decides what your query reads — and why small files are fatal.
idea: A columnar container lets a scan skip data at four levels: directories, row groups, columns, and pages. Parquet is a file format; Delta, Iceberg, and Hudi are table formats layered over those files.

sections.title: Row layout or column layout
sections.body:
There are two ways to lay a dataset out on disk: row by row, so one record's values sit together (Avro, JSON lines, CSV), or column by column, so one column's values across many rows sit together (Parquet, ORC).

The read pattern chooses the layout. Row-oriented files fit write-once, read-whole-record work: streaming ingest, Kafka payloads, log shipping, full-record lookups. Column-oriented files fit analytic work that scans a few columns across many rows — and they win three separate ways: only the projected columns' bytes are read, values of the same type sit next to each other and compress harder, and vectorized readers decode contiguous batches instead of walking row by row.

Both families are self-describing: the schema travels inside the file, so no external registry is needed to read it. And both are meant to be splittable at the container level — one file can back several parallel tasks — which is what lets Spark turn a single large file into distributed work.

Check the sources: Parquet file format · Spark: Parquet files · Spark: Avro files

sections.title: Inside a Parquet file
sections.body:
A Parquet file is a hierarchy, and that hierarchy explains nearly every tuning lever you have. The file is sliced horizontally into row groups; inside each row group, every column contributes a column chunk; each chunk is split into pages — the smallest unit of encoding, compression, and statistics.

The footer is the index: the schema, the byte offset of every column chunk, and per-chunk statistics such as minimum and maximum values. It is written after the data to allow single-pass writing, which is exactly why a reader starts at the end of the file — magic bytes, footer length, footer — and then reads only the chunks and pages it needs.

It is also why Parquet files are write-once: you never append a row group in place; new data becomes new files. Inside a page, values are encoded before compression. Dictionary encoding stores distinct values once and encodes rows as indexes — ideal for repetitive columns, but it falls back to plain encoding when the dictionary outgrows its budget, which is why a unique-ID column inflates file size. Optional bloom filters answer equality predicates on high-cardinality columns where min/max statistics cannot help.

Check the sources: Parquet file format · Parquet: encodings

sections.title: Reading less: pruning, sizes, and small files
sections.body:
A well-planned scan avoids data in four different ways, and each happens in a different place.

  • Partition pruning happens during directory listing, before any file is opened — directory names encode the values.
  • File and row-group skipping uses footer statistics: a predicate range that cannot intersect a chunk's min/max drops it entirely.
  • Column pruning uses chunk offsets: unreferenced columns are never read.
  • Predicate pushdown passes supported filters into the reader, so pages that cannot match can be skipped while decoding.

Structure matters more than flags: statistics cannot skip row groups if the data is unordered — every group's min/max spans the whole domain. Writing sorted or clustered data is what makes skipping work.

File count is the other lever. Spark packs file-scan input into partitions up to spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes (128 MiB default) and sizes post-shuffle partitions from AQE's advisory size; thousands of tiny files defeat both. Spark still packs small files into scan partitions, but charges each one spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes (4 MiB by default), so per-file opens, footer reads, and listing cost dominate, and each file's statistics are too small to skip anything. Rewriting the layout is the real fix.

Compression codecs — snappy (fast, the Spark default for Parquet), zstd (smaller, still fast), gzip (small but slow) — matter less than page independence: because Parquet compresses each page on its own, the container stays splittable regardless of codec. "A gzip file cannot be split" is a property of a raw gzip stream, not of gzip-compressed Parquet.

Check the sources: Spark: Parquet files and options · Spark: file partition sizing

sections.title: Schema evolution, and what a table format adds
sections.body:
Parquet resolves columns by name. Adding a column is safe — older files simply read as null for it — but renaming or dropping one is not, because old files still carry the old name. Type changes are safe only when they widen (int to long, float to double, higher decimal precision). Reading a directory whose files disagree on schema requires merging schemas across every footer (mergeSchema), which is off by default and can dominate startup on large tables.

None of this provides transactions, safe concurrent writers, or time travel: plain Parquet files on object storage have no commit protocol. That is the job of a table format. Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi layer a transaction log or metadata tree over the same Parquet files, defining which files are part of the table at each version. Iceberg replaces table metadata files with atomic swaps and tracks snapshots through manifest lists; Delta commits ordered log entries that add and remove files. Spark reads them through their own connectors — these projects are independent of the Spark 3.5.7 baseline, and their guarantees come from their own documentation.

Check the sources: Spark: schema merging · Iceberg table spec · Delta Lake documentation

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

events = spark.read.parquet("events")  # user_id, event_ts, amount, day

recent = (
    events
    .filter(F.col("day") == "2026-09-01")   # partition column: prunes directories
    .filter(F.col("amount") > 0)            # pushed into the Parquet reader
    .select("user_id", "amount")            # only these column chunks are read
)

recent.explain("formatted")
output: The formatted plan shows PartitionFilters for day and PushedFilters for amount, and the scan lists only the columns the query needs. How much is actually skipped depends on how the data is ordered and how the row groups are sized — that is what the statistics measure, so read the scan metrics rather than assuming a number.
pitfall: Treating Parquet as "just a smaller CSV". The format pays off only when scans can skip: an unpushable predicate, unordered data that defeats min/max statistics, or thousands of tiny files can leave a Parquet table as slow as the CSV it replaced.
question: A query filters on a column and still reads every row group. What do you check?
answer: Three things, in order. First, is the predicate pushable — a Python UDF, an unsupported expression, or a cast on the filtered column can block pushdown. Second, are the statistics useful — with unordered data every row group's min/max spans the whole domain, so nothing can be skipped; the fix is writing sorted or clustered data. Third, is it the partition column — only directory-level pruning avoids opening files at all. For equality filters on high-cardinality columns, bloom filters are the lever. All of these are write-time or layout decisions, not cluster-size decisions.

title: Delta Lake: transactions, MERGE & maintenance
dek: How an ordered log turns immutable Parquet files into a table, and what MERGE, OPTIMIZE, and VACUUM really cost.
idea: A Delta table is a set of immutable Parquet files plus an ordered log that says which files make up each version. Transactions, MERGE, time travel, and VACUUM are all changes to that file list, and every cost is a file rewritten or a file retained.

sections.title: The transaction log is the table
sections.body:
A Delta table is a directory of ordinary Parquet files, so everything in the storage-formats lesson still applies, plus a _delta_log/ directory that decides which of those files the table contains. Each commit is one file named by its zero-padded version (00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, and so on) holding newline-delimited JSON actions:

  • add: a data file joins the table, with its size, partition values, and per-file statistics (row count, min, max, null count).
  • remove: a file leaves the table. It is a tombstone with a deletion timestamp; the Parquet file stays on disk.
  • metaData and protocol: schema, partition columns, table properties, and the reader and writer features a client must support.
  • commitInfo: the operation, its parameters, the version it read, and its metrics. This is what DESCRIBE HISTORY shows.

Delta never edits a Parquet file. In the local run, deleting one row produced commit 1 with a remove for the four-row file and an add for a three-row replacement (numCopiedRows 3). A row-level change is a file swap in the log.

A reader builds a snapshot: it follows the _last_checkpoint pointer to the newest checkpoint, loads that Parquet file of replayed state, replays the JSON commits after it in version order, and keeps each file whose latest action is an add. Delta 3.2.1 writes a checkpoint every 10 commits by default (delta.checkpointInterval); the run's eleventh commit produced 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet, holding 11 live add rows plus the unexpired remove tombstone. The file list comes from the log rather than from listing data directories, and a query reads one version from start to finish.

Check the sources: Delta protocol · Delta 3.2.1 table property defaults

sections.title: Commits: optimistic concurrency and the storage underneath
sections.body:
Writers take no locks. A transaction reads a snapshot, writes new Parquet files that no reader can see yet, then validates and commits by creating the next log file. If another writer created that version first, the transaction checks the commits it missed against what it read and changed. With no conflict, it commits at the next free version; with a conflict, it fails. Per the Delta 3.2.1 docs, blind INSERTs cannot conflict with each other or with compaction; UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE can conflict with every operation type; compaction can conflict with those and with other compaction.

Two operations started together on one unpartitioned table (local run)
Concurrent pairObserved
INSERT + INSERT (blind appends), three roundsBoth committed every round; history shows each pair with the same readVersion
UPDATE + DELETEUPDATE committed; DELETE failed with ConcurrentAppendException
UPDATE + INSERT … SELECT from the same tableINSERT committed; UPDATE failed with ConcurrentAppendException

The message was [DELTA_CONCURRENT_APPEND] ConcurrentAppendException: Files were added to the root of the table by a concurrent update. Please try the operation again. The table was unpartitioned, so the loser's read covered every file and the winner's rewritten file counted as a concurrent append. Partitioning by the column both jobs filter on, and putting that predicate explicitly in each condition, keeps their file sets disjoint. The other conflict types are ConcurrentDeleteReadException (a file you read was removed), ConcurrentDeleteDeleteException (you both removed a file), MetadataChangedException, ProtocolChangedException, and ConcurrentTransactionException (two streaming queries sharing a checkpoint).

"Commits by atomically creating the next log file" is only as atomic as the storage. Delta requires atomic visibility, mutual exclusion (only one writer can create a given file), and consistent listing. The Delta 3.2.1 docs say HDFS and Azure storage give full guarantees for concurrent writers from multiple clusters, and GCS needs the correct LogStore configured. For S3, the docs state that S3 does not provide mutual exclusion and that concurrent writes from multiple Spark drivers can lead to data loss. Writes must come from a single driver, or every writer must use the experimental DynamoDB-backed io.delta.storage.S3DynamoDBLogStore. The log defines the transaction; the storage system decides whether the commit is truly exclusive.

Check the sources: Delta concurrency control · Delta storage configuration · Delta protocol

sections.title: MERGE: where the cost actually is
sections.body:
In Delta 3.2.1 a MERGE with matched clauses runs in three phases. First, an inner join of source and target on the merge condition finds the touched files, the target files holding at least one match, and checks that no target row matches two source rows. Second, it reads the touched files again and joins them with the source, writing updated rows, inserted rows, and every unmodified row in those files. Third, one commit removes the touched files and adds the new ones. Insert-only merges take a separate single-job path.

The draft's "two passes" is right about scanning the target twice, but the cost driver is rewrite volume: one match in a 1 GiB file rewrites the whole file. On a 100-row table in four 25-row files, one MERGE of five source rows (three matches in three different files, two inserts) reported:

DESCRIBE HISTORY operationMetrics for the same MERGE (local run)
MetricDefault (rewrite files)delta.enableDeletionVectors = true
numTargetFilesRemoved30
numTargetFilesAdded12
numTargetRowsUpdated33
numTargetRowsInserted22
numTargetRowsCopied720
numTargetDeletionVectorsAdded03
numOutputRows775

With deletion vectors, phase two writes only the changed rows. The touched files stay, re-added in the log with a deletionVector descriptor that marks their old rows as deleted. The trade-offs are real. Enabling the property upgraded the table to reader version 3 and writer version 7 with the deletionVectors feature, so clients without support can no longer read it. Readers also filter marked rows until OPTIMIZE or REORG TABLE … APPLY (PURGE) rewrites the files. The property defaults to false in Delta 3.2.1.

To shrink both phases, put a partition predicate in the ON condition so fewer files can match, keep files compacted and clustered on the merge key so matches land in few files, and size spark.sql.shuffle.partitions for the join. Deduplicate the source by key first: that is a correctness requirement, not a tuning option. (Databricks' "low shuffle merge" is a vendor-specific optimization, not part of OSS Delta 3.2.1.)

sections.title: Layout: statistics, partitioning, Z-order, and OPTIMIZE
sections.body:
Delta moves the file-skipping index into the log: every add carries min, max, and null counts, and a filter is checked against them before any data file is opened. Statistics cover the first 32 columns by default (delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols). A 34-column table in the run recorded statistics for c00 through c31 only, so a filter on a later column gets no file skipping unless you reorder columns or raise the setting.

Partitioning splits the table into directories by value. A filter on the partition column removes whole partitions from the file list, and partition predicates also keep concurrent writers apart. It suits low-cardinality columns that almost every query, DELETE, and MERGE filters on, such as a date. On a high-cardinality column it yields a flood of small files. Z-ordering (OPTIMIZE … ZORDER BY) instead rewrites files so rows with nearby values share files, narrowing each file's min/max range so statistics can skip on high-cardinality columns. It only helps columns with statistics, its locality weakens with each extra column, and it is not idempotent: each run re-clusters the files it considers, so bound it with WHERE on partition columns.

2,000 rows written as 40 tiny files; OPTIMIZE target size set to 8 KiB to force several outputs (local run)
LayoutFiles in tableFiles read for user_id BETWEEN 100 AND 120
Never optimized4040
OPTIMIZE (bin-packing)88
OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (user_id)71

Files read is the scan node's number of files read metric, and it matched a count of files whose logged min/max overlapped the range. Compaction alone fixed the file count but not the skipping; clustering fixed both. With the default target size (spark.databricks.delta.optimize.maxFileSize, 1 GiB), OPTIMIZE turned 40 files into 1, and a second run removed and added nothing. Compaction is idempotent, and readers on older snapshots keep reading the old files, which stay on disk until VACUUM. Delta 3.1 and later also offer optimized writes and auto compaction to create fewer small files in the first place; optimized writes are off by default.

sections.title: VACUUM, time travel, and RESTORE
sections.body:
VACUUM is what deletes data files; Delta never deletes them automatically. It removes files the current table version no longer references once they are older than the retention threshold, 7 days by default (delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration). The draft's "removes unreferenced files past retention" is close but loose: a file the latest version dropped an hour ago is unreferenced and still kept, because a version inside the window needs it. Log files are a separate clock: they are cleaned up after checkpoints once older than delta.logRetentionDuration (30 days by default).

That retention window is your time-travel and recovery window. Reading a version (versionAsOf, timestampAsOf, VERSION AS OF) needs both its log entries and its data files. VACUUM with less than the default retention is refused while spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled is true. The run's error began: "Are you sure you would like to vacuum files with such a low retention period? If you have writers that are currently writing to this table, there is a risk that you may corrupt the state of your Delta table." Short retention can delete files an in-flight writer or a long-running reader still needs, not only old history.

Scratch table, retention check disabled, VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS deleted the files of versions 0 and 1 (local run)
Action on version 0Observed
count()10: answered from log statistics; the physical plan was a LocalTableScan
collect()SparkFileNotFoundException: part-00000-….snappy.parquet does not exist
RESTORE TABLE … TO VERSION AS OF 0IllegalArgumentException: Not all files from version 0 are available in file system

RESTORE is itself a commit. On a table that had not been vacuumed, restoring version 0 wrote version 3, which removed the current file and re-added version 0's file (num_removed_files 1, num_restored_files 1), and history kept every earlier version. It rolls back the table's file list, not anything downstream consumers already read.

sections.title: Schema enforcement and evolution
sections.body:
Delta validates every write against the table schema: DataFrame columns must exist in the table, types must match, and names cannot differ only by case. In the run, appending a DataFrame with an extra tier column failed with AnalysisException: [_LEGACY_ERROR_TEMP_DELTA_0007] A schema mismatch detected when writing to the Delta table, and writing an integer into a string column failed with [DELTA_FAILED_TO_MERGE_FIELDS]. Evolution is opt-in:

  • mergeSchema set to true on an append or overwrite adds the new columns; the run's append then produced id, name, tier.
  • overwriteSchema replaces the schema during an overwrite.
  • MERGE follows the session setting spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled (default false).

MERGE is where schema drift goes quiet. With autoMerge off, whenMatchedUpdateAll() and whenNotMatchedInsertAll() succeeded and ignored the source's new tier column: the target stayed id, name, with no error. An explicit tier = s.tier assignment failed with [DELTA_MERGE_UNRESOLVED_EXPRESSION]. With autoMerge on, the same MERGE added tier, filled it for updated and inserted rows, and left it null in untouched rows. Enable it deliberately for the job that needs it, or add the column with ALTER TABLE first.

question: Two jobs update the same unpartitioned Delta table at the same moment. Walk through what each does, and why one of them fails.
answer: Both read the same snapshot, say version 11, and write new Parquet files that no reader can see yet. Each then tries to create 00000000000000000012.json. The storage system's mutual exclusion lets only one succeed, and that job becomes version 12. The other finds version 12 exists, reads it, and checks whether it added or removed files the losing transaction read or changed. An UPDATE's read covers the whole unpartitioned table, so the winner's rewritten file counts as a concurrent append, and the loser throws ConcurrentAppendException. Its written files stay unreferenced until VACUUM removes them. Two blind INSERTs would both commit, as versions 12 and 13. On S3 without a DynamoDB LogStore, that exclusion is not guaranteed across drivers.

diagram.alt: A Delta table as data files plus a transaction log. Data files part-A, part-C, and part-D are live; part-B is dashed because commit 1 removed it, though it stays on disk until VACUUM. The _delta_log holds ordered commits: 000…000.json adds A and B, 000…001.json removes B and adds C, commits 2 to 9 follow, 000…010.checkpoint.parquet stores the full state at version 10, and 000…011.json adds D. A reader reads _last_checkpoint, loads checkpoint 10, replays commit 11, and keeps the latest adds, so snapshot 11 is files A, C, and D. Below, two writers that both read version 11 try to create 000…012.json: writer 1's put-if-absent succeeds and becomes version 12; writer 2 finds the file exists, re-checks for conflicts, and retries as version 13 or throws.
diagram.caption: The log, not the directory, defines the table. A checkpoint shortcuts replay, and the commit race is decided by the storage system's put-if-absent guarantee.
