title: Structured Streaming: micro-batches, state & exactly-once
dek: What the driver plans each trigger, what the checkpoint records, and why late data and restarts behave the way they do.
idea: A streaming query is a sequence of small batch queries over new offsets. Exactly-once comes from logging each batch's offsets before it runs and its commit after the sink finishes, so a failed batch replays the same range into a sink that tolerates the replay.

sections.title: The unbounded table and the micro-batch loop
sections.body:
Structured Streaming models a stream as an input table that only grows: every arriving record is a new row. You write an ordinary DataFrame query against that table, and the engine keeps the result table up to date without ever materializing the input. Each trigger reads only the data that arrived since the previous batch, combines it with the intermediate state the query kept, writes what changed to a sink, and discards the source rows.

The driver owns the loop. For micro-batch N it asks each source for its latest available offsets, writes the chosen range to the checkpoint, and plans the batch as a normal Spark SQL execution (an IncrementalExecution in the source), so Catalyst, shuffles, stages, and tasks all apply per batch. Executor tasks read exactly that range, run the operators, load and save state-store versions for stateful operators, and write the sink output. When the batch finishes, the driver records it as committed and plans N+1.

Stateful queries also run no-data batches: batches with zero input rows whose only job is to advance the watermark, emit finished results, and evict state. In the watermark runs behind this lesson, a no-data batch followed each data batch that raised the watermark — for example batch 1, with 0 rows, running at a watermark of 11:57.

The word “checkpoint” means something different here than in cache and recovery: a streaming checkpoint is one query's progress log plus its state, not lineage truncation for a batch DataFrame.

Check the sources: Structured Streaming guide: input and result tables · MicroBatchExecution source

sections.title: Triggers decide when a batch starts
sections.body:
A trigger controls timing, not what a batch contains. Every micro-batch trigger still plans, runs, and commits batches the same way.

Trigger types in Spark 3.5.7
TriggerWhen batches runUse it for
None set (default)The next micro-batch starts as soon as the previous one finishes; the PySpark API describes it as equivalent to processingTime='0 seconds'.Lowest micro-batch latency on an always-on cluster.
processingTime='1 minute'At interval boundaries. A batch that overruns is followed immediately; if no new data is available, no batch starts.Predictable batch cadence and sink load.
availableNow=TrueProcesses all data available at start, possibly in several batches that respect source limits such as maxFilesPerTrigger. Uncommitted batches run first, the watermark advances per batch, a final no-data batch runs if needed, then the query stops.Scheduled incremental jobs that start, catch up, and exit.
once=True (deprecated)One batch with everything available, then stop. The guide deprecates it in favor of availableNow; PySpark 3.5.7 printed no warning when it was used locally.Existing jobs only; migrate them.
continuous='1 second' (experimental)Long-running tasks read and write continuously; the interval is how often progress is checkpointed.Millisecond-latency map-like pipelines that can accept duplicates.

Continuous processing is a different engine, not a faster trigger. The guide quotes latencies around 1 ms against about 100 ms at best for micro-batches, but the part interviewers probe is the guarantee: continuous mode is at-least-once. It supports only map-like operations (projections and selections; SQL functions except aggregations, current_timestamp(), and current_date()), the Kafka and rate sources, and the Kafka, memory, and console sinks. It needs a core for every source partition, does not retry failed tasks automatically, and cannot use foreachBatch. Locally, a rate-source filter into a memory sink ran under a continuous trigger; an aggregation failed with Continuous processing does not support Aggregate operations, and a file source was rejected the same way.

Check the sources: Guide: triggers · PySpark DataStreamWriter.trigger · Guide: continuous processing

sections.title: Exactly-once: replayable sources, the checkpoint, idempotent sinks
sections.body:
End-to-end exactly-once is not one atomic commit. It comes from replaying a batch deterministically after a failure into a sink that tolerates the replay. The write order in MicroBatchExecution is:

  1. The driver writes offsets/N: the write-ahead record of the batch's source offsets, plus the batch watermark, batch timestamp, and a few pinned settings.
  2. Tasks process that range; stateful operators write the next state version under state/.
  3. The sink writes the batch output.
  4. The driver writes commits/N.

On restart Spark compares the latest offsets entry with the latest commit: a committed batch moves the query to N+1, an uncommitted one is re-run over the same offsets. After two batches of a stateless file-to-Parquet query, the checkpoint held metadata, offsets/0, offsets/1, commits/0, commits/1, sources/0/0, and sources/0/1 — the last two recording which input file each batch took. Stateful queries add state/. A restart on that checkpoint with no new files read zero rows; adding one file read exactly one.

Replay only helps when both ends cooperate:

  • The source must be replayable. The file source (files moved into the directory atomically) and Kafka qualify. The Kafka source keeps its offsets in the checkpoint and does not commit them to Kafka, and data that has aged out of the topic cannot be replayed (failOnDataLoss). The socket source is not fault-tolerant. Kafka behavior here is documentation-reviewed only.
  • The sink must be idempotent or transactional. The file sink is documented as exactly-once; the Kafka and foreach sinks are at-least-once; console and memory are not fault-tolerant; foreachBatch is as safe as your function. Delta table writes are covered in Delta Lake.

foreachBatch passes each batch as a DataFrame plus its batchId; a replayed batch carries the same id and, for a deterministic query, the same rows. In a crash test after the write but before commits/1, a plain Parquet append duplicated the replayed row, while a Delta write keyed by the batch id skipped it:

PYTHON / PYSPARK
def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    (batch_df.write.format("delta").mode("append")
        .option("txnAppId", "orders-to-silver")   # stable for this checkpoint
        .option("txnVersion", batch_id)           # a replayed batch is skipped
        .save(target_path))

query = (orders.writeStream.foreachBatch(write_batch)
         .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
         .trigger(availableNow=True).start())
query.awaitTermination()

If the function writes the batch more than once, persist it first: without that, a two-row batch reported numInputRows of 6 because it was computed three times.

Check the sources: MicroBatchExecution: offset and commit logs · Guide: fault-tolerance semantics · Guide: sources and sinks · Guide: foreachBatch · Kafka integration guide · Delta Lake: idempotent writes in foreachBatch

sections.title: State, watermarks, and output modes
sections.body:
Streaming aggregations, dropDuplicates, stream-stream joins, and mapGroupsWithState/flatMapGroupsWithState keep state between batches in a versioned state store: by default in executor JVM memory backed by checkpoint files, or with the RocksDB provider in native memory and local disk. State shrinks only when something tells the engine a key can no longer change. That is the watermark's job.

How the watermark moves. At the end of a batch the engine takes the maximum event time it has seen and subtracts the withWatermark delay; the next batch uses that value. It follows event time, not the wall clock, so if data stops the watermark stops. With several watermarked inputs the global watermark is the minimum by default (spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy).

When late data is dropped. The documented guarantee runs one way: a row within the delay is never dropped, and an older row may or may not be. For a windowed aggregation Spark's test is the window's end, not the row's timestamp. With a 10-minute delay and 5-minute windows:

  • Rows at 12:01, 12:02, and 12:07 set the watermark to 11:57. A later batch with 12:20 and a late 12:03 still counted 12:03 (the 12:00 window became 3), then the watermark moved to 12:10.
  • A 12:04 row arriving next was dropped: its window ended at 12:05, not after 12:10. numRowsDroppedByWatermark reported 1.
  • In a separate run with the watermark at 12:12, a 12:11:30 row was still counted because its window ends at 12:15, while a 12:09 row was dropped.

Watermarks evict aggregation state only in append or update mode, only when the aggregation groups by the watermarked column or a window on it, and only when withWatermark comes before the aggregation.

QueryAllowed modesWhat you see
No aggregation (select, filter, stream-static join)Append; update behaves the sameEach new row once. Complete mode raised AnalysisException locally.
Aggregation without a watermarkUpdate, completeAppend raised AnalysisException locally. State is never evicted.
Event-time aggregation with a watermarkAppend, update, completeAppend emits each window once, after the watermark passes its end; update emits changed windows every batch; complete re-emits everything and evicts nothing.
Stream-stream joinAppendUpdate mode raised AnalysisException locally.
mapGroupsWithState / flatMapGroupsWithStateUpdate / the mode the operator declaresDocumentation-reviewed only.

For deduplication where a retried event carries a new timestamp, Spark 3.5 adds dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark: it keys on the id alone and keeps state only while copies can still fall within the watermark delay.

sections.title: What you may change on the same checkpoint
sections.body:
A restart on the same checkpoint reuses the stored offsets, commits, and state, so the new query must still fit them. The guide's “Recovery Semantics after Changes in a Streaming Query” sorts changes into allowed (possible, with semantics that depend on the query) and not allowed (the restarted query is likely to fail with unpredictable errors).

  • Allowed: adding or removing filters; projections with the same output schema; adding, removing, or changing rate limits such as maxOffsetsPerTrigger; changing a Kafka output topic; changing foreach writer code or the code inside a state-mapping function.
  • Not allowed: changing the number or type of sources; generally, changing subscribed topics or files; changing a file sink's output path; changing any stateful operation's schema — grouping keys or aggregates, deduplication columns, stream-stream join columns or join type, user state schema or timeout type.
  • Fixed at the first run: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (state is hash-partitioned by key), the state store provider class, and the multiple-watermark policy. Each offsets/N records them, and on restart Spark overwrites the session value with the recorded one.

Do not treat a successful restart as proof that a change was safe. Spark compares the stored state schema with the new one by field count, data types, and nullability compatibility, not by field names. On one checkpoint, changing count() to sum("amount") failed with StateSchemaNotCompatible, and so did adding a second grouping key. Swapping groupBy("city") for groupBy("country") — still one string key — ran without error, and a row with country “Delhi” came out with count 2 because it reused the old city key's state. Adding a filter in front of the same aggregation worked as documented.

Check the sources: Guide: recovery semantics after changes · Guide: configurations fixed after the first run · OffsetSeq source: pinned configurations

sections.title: Reading lastProgress
sections.body:
query.lastProgress returns the most recent StreamingQueryProgress (a dictionary in Python), and query.recentProgress keeps the last few. Read several entries, not one.

  • id stays the same across restarts from one checkpoint — locally it matched the value in metadata. runId identifies one start of the query, and batchId is the micro-batch number.
  • numInputRows, inputRowsPerSecond (the rate data is arriving), and processedRowsPerSecond (the rate Spark is processing it).
  • durationMs: latestOffset and getBatch for source discovery, queryPlanning, walCommit and commitOffsets for the offset and commit logs, addBatch for running the batch and writing the sink, and triggerExecution for the whole trigger.
  • eventTime: watermark, plus max, min, and avg event time when the batch has rows.
  • stateOperators: numRowsTotal, numRowsUpdated, numRowsRemoved, numRowsDroppedByWatermark, memoryUsedBytes, and provider-specific customMetrics.
  • sources: startOffset, endOffset, latestOffset, and per-source rates.

A query that is falling behind shows processedRowsPerSecond staying below inputRowsPerSecond, or triggerExecution longer than the trigger interval. Then find where the time goes: a large addBatch points at processing or the sink, a growing numRowsTotal points at state, and slow walCommit or commitOffsets points at checkpoint storage. Two cautions from local runs: the file source reported latestOffset as null, and a continuous-mode query reported no progress at all.

import json, os, tempfile
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC")
base = tempfile.mkdtemp()
events_dir, checkpoint = os.path.join(base, "events"), os.path.join(base, "checkpoint")
os.makedirs(events_dir)

def add_file(name, times):
    tmp = os.path.join(base, name)
    with open(tmp, "w") as f:
        f.writelines(json.dumps({"ts": t}) + "\n" for t in times)
    os.rename(tmp, os.path.join(events_dir, name))  # atomic move into the source

counts = (
    spark.readStream.schema("ts TIMESTAMP").json(events_dir)
    .withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("ts", "5 minutes"))
    .count()
)

def show_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    rows = batch_df.select(F.date_format("window.start", "HH:mm").alias("start"), "count").collect()
    print("batch", batch_id, sorted((r.start, r["count"]) for r in rows))

def run_until_caught_up():
    query = (counts.writeStream.outputMode("update").foreachBatch(show_batch)
             .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint)
             .trigger(availableNow=True).start())
    query.awaitTermination()
    for p in query.recentProgress:
        print("  progress", p["batchId"], "rows", p["numInputRows"],
              "watermark", p["eventTime"]["watermark"][11:16],
              "dropped", p["stateOperators"][0]["numRowsDroppedByWatermark"])

add_file("1.json", ["2026-09-15T12:01:00Z", "2026-09-15T12:02:00Z", "2026-09-15T12:07:00Z"])
run_until_caught_up()
add_file("2.json", ["2026-09-15T12:20:00Z", "2026-09-15T12:03:00Z"])
run_until_caught_up()
add_file("3.json", ["2026-09-15T12:04:00Z"])
run_until_caught_up()

Run 2 restarted on the same checkpoint and read only 2.json: batch 2 printed [('12:00', 3), ('12:20', 1)], so the late 12:03 row was counted, and no-data batch 3 ran at watermark 12:10. Run 3 printed an empty batch 4 with dropped 1, because the 12:04 row's window ended at 12:05. The watermark column shows the value each batch ran with, as UTC HH:MM. Batch numbers include no-data batches, which Spark schedules itself, so treat them as observed rather than guaranteed.

pitfall: Treating a restart that succeeds as a change that is safe. Spark matches stored state to the new plan by field count, type, and nullability, not names, so replacing one string grouping key with another string key restarts cleanly and silently merges unrelated state. Plan stateful schema changes as a new checkpoint (and, for idempotent Delta writers, a new txnAppId), with a backfill if the history matters.
question: A query crashes after its sink wrote micro-batch 7 but before commits/7 existed. What happens on restart, and what must be true for the output to stay exactly-once?
answer: offsets/7 exists without commits/7, so the restarted query re-runs batch 7 over exactly the offsets recorded in offsets/7 instead of asking the source for new data, and stateful operators start again from the state version that batch 7 began with. The sink receives batch 7 a second time. Output stays exactly-once only if the source can still serve that range (the files are still there, or Kafka still retains those offsets) and the sink recognizes the replay: the file sink's own log, a Delta write keyed by txnAppId and txnVersion, or a MERGE on a business key. A plain append or a Kafka write produces duplicates.

diagram.alt: One micro-batch N. The driver finds the source offset range, writes offsets/N to the checkpoint, and plans an incremental batch. Executor tasks read exactly that range; stateful operators load and save versioned state in the state store inside the checkpoint; the sink writes the output. Only after the sink succeeds does the driver write commits/N. An offsets entry without a matching commit means batch N is re-run.
diagram.caption: One micro-batch in Spark 3.5.7. The offsets entry is written before the work and the commit entry after the sink, so a crash in between replays the same range. Continuous processing uses a different engine.

title: The complete Spark execution flow
dek: From spark-submit to the final result: explain who does what, when, and why.
idea: Tell two connected stories: how the application gets compute, and how a query turns a plan into work on that compute.

sections.title: Before you draw the flow
sections.body:
Open with a scope statement: “I’ll describe a classic PySpark batch application using DataFrames on Spark 3.5.7.” Then separate the application’s lifetime from the execution of an individual query. One application can run many queries and jobs.

This matters in interviews: a notebook may already have a session and compute attached. With Spark Connect, a client sends plans to a remote server; the Python client is not the classic driver described below. Structured Streaming adds a continuously running query and its own execution lifecycle.

Learn the fundamentals first if the terms are new. This is the capstone that connects them.

Check the source: Spark Connect has a separate client/server architecture · Application components and resource allocation

sections.title: 1–4 · Start the application
sections.body:
1. Submit the program. A command such as spark-submit app.py launches the application using its master and deployment configuration. In client mode the driver runs on the submitting side; in cluster mode the cluster infrastructure launches it. The deployment mode determines driver placement.
  2. Initialize or reuse the session. Driver-side code obtains a SparkSession. In classic Spark, it uses a SparkContext for the application’s connection and scheduling machinery. getOrCreate() may return an existing session; it is not a command that always launches a fresh driver.
  3. Acquire executor resources. Cluster-manager-specific integration requests resources. YARN, Kubernetes, and Spark standalone are common choices; Mesos is deprecated in this reference release. Executors are processes, not synonyms for worker machines. Memory requests also have overhead beyond the configured executor heap.
  4. Register and become schedulable. Executors connect back to the driver. Resource availability and readiness settings affect when scheduling begins. There is no universal rule that every requested executor must exist before work can start. Dynamic allocation can add or remove executors later.

In local mode, task threads run locally; there is no remote cluster-manager allocation of three separate executors. In an already attached notebook, much of this startup may have happened before your cell ran.

Check the source: Driver placement and spark-submit · SparkSession.getOrCreate: create or reuse · Application components and resource allocation · Scheduling and dynamic resource allocation · Task CPUs, registration readiness, and retry configuration

sections.title: 5–8 · Describe the query and plan it
sections.body:
1. Run the driver-side program. Python control flow executes normally. Reading a table and building expressions such as filter and groupBy describe a distributed computation. Metadata discovery, schema inference, and analysis can already do work or report errors.
  2. Analyze the logical plan. Spark SQL resolves references to columns, relations, functions, and types. “Aggregate over a filter over an input relation” describes the requested result. A logical input relation is not yet a physical FileScan operator.
  3. Optimize the logical plan. Applicable rules simplify expressions and reduce unnecessary work. Column pruning and eligible filter pushdown are useful examples. Pushdown depends on the source and predicate; a remaining filter may still need to run. Join reordering and strategy choices have eligibility, statistics, and configuration requirements.
  4. Choose and prepare physical operators. The physical plan specifies how to compute the result: scans, filters, partial/final aggregates, joins, and exchanges. Eligible operators can be fused into generated code. That fusion is distinct from a scheduler stage.

These are conceptual planning phases, not an eager timeline for every transformation. Query execution holds lazily evaluated planning results; an action or plan inspection can demand them. explain("extended") lets you inspect the representations before requesting result rows.

Catalyst plans structured queries. The DAG scheduler later works with execution dependencies; it does not schedule the Catalyst logical tree directly. Ordinary RDD transformations do not go through the same DataFrame/SQL optimization pipeline.

Check the source: QueryExecution: analysis, optimization, physical planning · Reading EXPLAIN output · Physical strategy selection and join eligibility

sections.title: 9–11 · Request results and schedule work
sections.body:
1. Call an action. show(), count(), collect(), or an actual write operation asks for an outcome. Accessing df.write alone only creates a writer. Necessary planning is completed and execution work is submitted. One user action can lead to multiple scheduler jobs; query execution and job are different levels.
  2. Build the stage dependencies and tasks. The DAG scheduler identifies shuffle dependencies and available intermediate results. For a runnable stage attempt, it creates the required tasks and submits them as a TaskSet. A ShuffleMapStage produces shuffle output; a ResultStage produces the result requested by that job.
  3. Place task attempts on executors. The task scheduler uses resource offers, locality preferences, scheduling policy, and task resource requirements. The scheduler backend dispatches the selected work to executors. The cluster manager supplies resources; it is not an obligatory relay for each task or each data row.

Say “one task per partition to compute in that stage attempt”, not “one task per original file.” Some actions need only a subset of partitions. Retries and speculation create additional attempts, and downstream partition counts can change.

CPU-only illustration: three executors, four available cores each
Task CPU requestAvailable task slots16 ready tasks need at least
spark.task.cpus = 13 × floor(4 / 1) = 122 waves
spark.task.cpus = 23 × floor(4 / 2) = 63 waves

This is a capacity model, not a timing promise. Other resources, competing jobs, skew, and task durations matter. Tasks run on executor threads; Spark does not permanently pin a partition to a physical CPU core.

Check the source: Actions, lazy transformations, and recomputation · DAGScheduler: stages, tasks, TaskSets, and recovery · TaskSchedulerImpl: task placement and resource offers · Task CPUs, registration readiness, and retry configuration

sections.title: 12–14 · Process partitions and shuffle
sections.body:
1. Execute the task’s computation. An executor deserializes task information and processes the assigned execution partition. Pipelined operators can read, filter, project, and partly aggregate within one task. Built-in SQL expressions run through Spark’s execution engine; Python UDFs can involve Python worker processes.
  2. Produce and fetch shuffle blocks when required. For a grouped sum, map-side tasks may first produce partial sums. A shuffle exchange distributes these by key. The same key must reach compatible downstream grouping, but multiple distinct keys can share a hash partition. Downstream tasks fetch the required blocks, locally or remotely.
  3. Run downstream operators; adapt when applicable. Once dependencies are available, downstream tasks complete the aggregation. With AQE enabled, materialized exchange statistics can inform changes such as coalescing shuffle partitions or selecting a different supported join strategy. Initial and final plans can differ.

Shuffle can involve serialization, disk I/O, network I/O, and spill. A network transfer is not required for every block. BroadcastExchange instead prepares and distributes a broadcast relation; treating every operator containing “Exchange” as a shuffle is inaccurate.

Locality tries to avoid avoidable movement. PROCESS_LOCAL, NODE_LOCAL, RACK_LOCAL, and ANY describe locality choices; NO_PREF means there is no locality preference. Object-storage reads do not imply that an executor lives beside an HDFS block.

Check the source: Shuffle dependencies and output partitioning · BroadcastExchange is a different exchange · Adaptive query execution and shuffle partition coalescing · Data locality and its trade-offs

An AQE query stage is a physical-plan unit around an exchange; a whole-stage codegen region is an operator-fusion unit. Neither is interchangeable with a DAG scheduler stage in the Jobs/Stages UI. See the AQE query-stage implementation.

sections.title: 15–17 · Observe, recover, and finish
sections.body:
1. Track progress throughout execution. Task status updates and metrics feed the driver’s view of the application. Use the SQL tab for query plans and linked jobs; use stage/task views for skew, shuffle, spill, duration, and GC evidence. The Storage tab concerns materialized persisted data.
  2. Recover eligible failures. A failed task attempt may be retried within configured limits. Lost shuffle output can require recomputation of earlier work. Recovery needs available inputs and recomputable logic; a deterministic code error will not be repaired by simply retrying it. Driver failure is a different lifecycle problem, not a task retry.
  3. Return or commit the output. show() brings back enough rows to display, although computing those rows can require substantial upstream work. collect() returns all result rows to the driver. Distributed file writes normally write data from executors and coordinate commits; output data need not pass through the driver. One executor does not imply one output file. The application can accept another action, or terminate and release resources.

Do not claim that external side effects happen exactly once merely because Spark retries tasks. Side-effect safety and a sink’s commit guarantees need their own design. Do not stop a shared notebook session just because one query has finished.

Check the source: SQL, Jobs, Stages, Executors, and Storage tabs · DAGScheduler: stages, tasks, TaskSets, and recovery · Actions, lazy transformations, and recomputation

sections.title: Trace the example before running it
sections.body:
The runnable example below creates 12 rows in four input partitions. Each ID determines a country and an amount. Filtering amount > 100 keeps IDs 3–11. Here is the input-side arithmetic:

Initial range partitions and surviving amounts
PartitionInput IDsAfter the filter
P00, 1, 2No surviving rows
P13, 4, 5India 150 · USA 200 · UK 250
P26, 7, 8India 300 · USA 350 · UK 400
P39, 10, 11India 450 · USA 500 · UK 550

In a typical full-input execution, each input partition needs a task, even P0: Spark must evaluate its rows before knowing none survive. Partial sums can be shuffled and merged to produce India 900, USA 1050, UK 1200. The output order is unspecified.

CONCEPTUAL PHYSICAL FLOW · READ TOP TO BOTTOM
Range (4 input partitions)
  → Filter amount > 100
  → Partial aggregate by country
  → Shuffle exchange by country
  → Final aggregate
  → Display a small result

This sketches the aggregation’s shuffle boundary, not an assertion that show() must produce exactly one job and two stages. AQE and result retrieval influence the observed scheduler work. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions does not define the four input partitions in this example.

For your Parquet version, replace the generated input with spark.read.parquet("/orders"). Inspect the actual scan and partitioning instead of assuming one input file means one task. Look for pushed filters and selected columns; do not expect a literal operator-for-operator match with this range example.

sections.title: A repeatable way to answer in an interview
sections.body:
1. Scope it. State classic PySpark or Spark Connect, batch or streaming, and whether the application is already running.
  2. Draw the roles. Put the driver beside the cluster manager and executors. Show resource allocation separately from task dispatch and data access.
  3. Walk the query. Use one scan → filter → grouped sum → action example. Identify what is a plan and what actually processes data.
  4. Explain the expensive boundary. Draw the partial aggregate, shuffle write/read, and final aggregate. Say what crosses the boundary.
  5. Size the work with assumptions. Separate input partitions, shuffle partitions, task attempts, and concurrent slots. Then discuss skew and retries.
  6. Verify the story. Name the plan operator or Spark UI evidence you would inspect. Finish with where the result goes and whether the application stays alive.

Practice at two depths: give the answer below in roughly 90 seconds, then walk through the example when the interviewer asks for detail. Avoid reciting 17 steps without explaining who owns each step.

sections.title: Corrections to the supplied explanation
sections.body:
The supplied answer is a useful starting outline. These changes make it safer to use as an interview explanation:

Shortcut in the draftMore accurate explanation
Session/context → driver startsThe driver-side program creates or reuses the classic session/context. Driver placement comes from deployment mode; attached notebooks may already have it.
Nothing runs until an actionResult computation is generally lazy. Python code, metadata work, and analysis can run earlier; plan inspection can demand planning.
Every transformation produces a physical plan immediatelyLogical expressions are composed; analysis, optimization, and physical planning are requested as needed.
Task scheduler creates the tasksDAG scheduling creates the tasks and TaskSet for a stage attempt. Task scheduling places and manages task attempts.
One action → one jobA useful first approximation, not a count guarantee. SQL actions can involve multiple jobs.
Exchange → shuffleDistinguish shuffle exchanges from broadcast exchanges.
join is always wide; withColumn is always narrowInspect required physical distribution. Broadcast joins can avoid shuffling the large side; a window expression introduced with withColumn can require redistribution.
Core → one taskTask slots depend on CPU/resource requests and available resources. The default CPU request is one; it is configurable.
Each distinct key gets its own partitionHash partitioning places the same key compatibly, but different keys may share a partition.
The selected physical plan never changesAQE can revise parts of the plan using runtime statistics.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Uses an existing classic SparkSession named spark.
orders = (
    spark.range(0, 12, 1, 4)
    .withColumn("country",
        F.when(F.col("id") % 3 == 0, "India")
         .when(F.col("id") % 3 == 1, "USA")
         .otherwise("UK"))
    .withColumn("amount", F.col("id") * 50)
)
result = (
    orders.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)
    .groupBy("country")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))

result.explain("extended")  # inspect plans, not result rows

pitfall: The physical plan, scheduler-stage graph, and task-attempt timeline are different views. Do not infer exact job counts from source lines, or exact concurrency from partition counts.
question: Can you explain the full Spark flow, from application startup to the final result?
answer: For a classic PySpark batch application, submission and deploy mode determine where the driver runs. Driver-side code creates or reuses a SparkSession and SparkContext, and cluster integration obtains executors that register with the driver. DataFrame operations describe a logical query; Spark SQL analyzes it and, when needed, optimizes and plans physical execution. An action requests results and can trigger multiple jobs. The DAG scheduler separates execution dependencies at shuffle boundaries and creates tasks for runnable stage partitions. The task scheduler places task attempts on available executor resources through its backend. Executors run operators, may partly aggregate, and exchange data when the plan requires it. AQE can adjust downstream execution using runtime statistics. Status and metrics return to the driver, recoverable failures can be retried, and the output is returned to the driver or written to storage. The application can then run more work or shut down.

practice.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")

    practice.range(0, 12, 1, 4)

sections.title: Set the rules before you count
sections.body:
Start after Predict what Spark will do. These eight exercises come from a supplied, ChatGPT-generated study sheet of ten “count the jobs, stages, and tasks” questions. Two near-duplicate pairs are merged. The sheet’s answers were not used. Every answer here was derived from Spark 3.5.7 source and documentation and then measured. They are practice questions, not reported interview questions.

  • Job: one scheduler run, started by an action or by Spark itself. Spark starts its own jobs for things like schema inference, broadcast collection, AQE shuffle stages, and each round of show().
  • Stage: tasks that run the same code without crossing a shuffle. A job can list a skipped stage. Its shuffle output already existed, so none of its tasks ran. Count skipped stages separately.
  • Task: one partition’s work in one stage. A task attempt is one try at that task. Failures and speculation add attempts, not tasks.

The counts depend on more than the code. They change with the Spark version, whether AQE is on (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled, true by default since 3.2.0), spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (200 by default), the broadcast threshold, how many files you read and how big they are, and schema options on the reader. They also depend on how many rows show() needs and where those rows sit, and on cached data. Interviewers usually picture AQE off, so each exercise reports both.

How these numbers were measured. Local PySpark 3.5.7, local[4] (default parallelism 4), JDK 17. Each exercise ran in a fresh application under each configuration. setJobGroup tagged the jobs for each line. While the application was running, the Spark UI REST API gave the jobs, their stage IDs, each stage’s status and task count, and each stage’s task attempts. Every measurement ran twice with identical counts. Job and stage IDs themselves vary between runs, so do not memorize them.

This setup is for local mode on your own machine. fresh_session() stops the running application and starts a clean local[4] one. Nothing cached and no shuffle output carries over, and job IDs start again from 0. Do not call it on a shared cluster or in a managed notebook. There, keep one session and rely on label() job groups. import json

# Local mode only: fresh_session() stops the current application.
BASE = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "count-spark-work")

ORDERS_PARQUET = f"{BASE}/orders_parquet"  # 4 Parquet files

def fresh_session(aqe=True):
    """Stop any running application and start a clean local[4] one."""
    active = SparkSession.getActiveSession()
    if active is not None:
        active.stop()
    elif SparkContext._active_spark_context is not None:
        SparkContext._active_spark_context.stop()
    return (
        SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]")
        .appName("count-spark-work")
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", str(aqe).lower())
        .config("spark.ui.showConsoleProgress", "false")
        .getOrCreate()
    )


def label(name):
    """Attribute every job started from here on to one job group."""
    SparkSession.getActiveSession().sparkContext.setJobGroup(name, name)


def print_work(group):
    """Print jobs, stages, and task attempts for one job group (REST API)."""
    sc = SparkSession.getActiveSession().sparkContext
    base = f"{sc.uiWebUrl}/api/v1/applications/{sc.applicationId}"
    opener = urllib.request.build_opener(urllib.request.ProxyHandler({}))

    def get(path):
        with opener.open(base + path) as response:
            return json.load(response)

    jobs, previous = [], None
    for _ in range(50):  # the UI store updates asynchronously
        jobs = [j for j in get("/jobs") if j.get("jobGroup") == group]
        done = all(j["status"] != "RUNNING" for j in jobs)
        if jobs and done and len(jobs) == previous:
            break
        previous = len(jobs)
        time.sleep(0.2)
    totals = dict(jobs=len(jobs), stages=0, skipped=0, tasks=0, attempts=0)
    for job in sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j["jobId"]):
        print(f"job {job['jobId']} {job['status']}: {job['name'].split(' at ')[0]}")
        for stage_id in sorted(job["stageIds"]):
            for stage in get(f"/stages/{stage_id}"):
                if stage["status"] == "SKIPPED":
                    totals["skipped"] += 1
                    print(f"  stage {stage_id}: skipped ({stage['numTasks']} tasks not run)")
                    continue
                path = f"/stages/{stage_id}/{stage['attemptId']}/taskList?length=100000"
                attempts = len(get(path))
                totals["stages"] += 1
                totals["tasks"] += stage["numTasks"]
                totals["attempts"] += attempts
                print(f"  stage {stage_id}.{stage['attemptId']}: {stage['numTasks']} tasks, "
                      f"{attempts} attempts, {stage['status']}")
    print(f"{group}: {totals['jobs']} jobs, {totals['stages']} stages run, "
          f"{totals['skipped']} skipped, {totals['tasks']} tasks, {totals['attempts']} attempts")

sections.title: How many input tasks? Files, bytes, and maxPartitionBytes
sections.body:
A file scan stage runs one task per file partition. File partitions are not files. Spark caps a split at maxSplitBytes = min(maxPartitionBytes, max(openCostInBytes, bytesPerCore)). Here bytesPerCore is the total input bytes, plus a 4 MB openCostInBytes for each file, divided by spark.sql.files.minPartitionNum. That setting defaults to the default parallelism, which is 4 here. Spark cuts large splittable files into splits of that size. It sorts the splits largest first, then packs them into partitions, counting the open cost for each split.

Tiny files make maxSplitBytes 4 MB, and each file plus its open cost fills a partition on its own. So four small files gave four tasks and one gave one. Changing maxPartitionBytes changes the task count only once files outgrow the computed split size. The table shows full scans of CSV data with a supplied schema (a noop write).

For the 78 MB file, bytesPerCore is (78,223,899 + 4,194,304) ÷ 4, about 19.6 MiB. Under the 128 MB default that is the split size, which gives 4 partitions. A 16 MiB cap gives 5, and a 2 MiB cap gives 38. Sorting splits largest first also decides which rows show() sees first: the first partition holds the largest file, not the first one written.

  • CSV: the reader runs take(1) for the first line, which gives column names or the column count. That is a one-task job. inferSchema adds one extra pass over the sampled input. At the default samplingRatio of 1.0 that is every row, one task per input partition.
  • JSON: without a schema, inference reads the records, all of them at the default samplingRatio of 1.0. That is one job over every input partition.
  • Parquet: types come from file footers. Even for a single file, Spark 3.5.7 read the footer in a small distributed job, not on the driver. Without mergeSchema it read one footer, so one task. With mergeSchema it read all four, so four tasks, with parallelism capped at the default parallelism.

A supplied schema started no job for any reader, and these jobs happen before the query you care about. So when someone asks how many jobs a snippet runs, first ask whether it infers a schema.

sections.title: A repeatable counting method
sections.body:
1. List the reads. Schema inference, the CSV first line, and Parquet footers can each add a job before the action.
  2. Find each action and how it collects rows. count(), collect(), and writes process every partition. show(n) and take(n) ask for n+1 or n rows. They scan one partition first, then more in rounds (each round up to 4× the partitions scanned so far), and every round is a separate job.
  3. Find the exchanges in explain(). A hash or single-partition Exchange is a shuffle boundary. With AQE off, one job has one stage per shuffle plus a result stage. BroadcastExchange is not a stage boundary. It collects the small side in its own job first.
  4. With AQE on, split the job. Each shuffle stage (and, in 3.5, a cached relation) is materialized as its own job. The final job then lists those stages as skipped and runs on the partitions AQE produced, often coalesced.
  5. Count tasks per stage. A scan stage has one task per file partition, or one per partition for a cache or RDD. A post-shuffle stage has one per shuffle partition: 200, the explicit repartition number, or AQE’s coalesced count. Incremental show() runs fewer.
  6. Measure and state the conditions. Tag the work with job groups. Report jobs, stages run, stages skipped, tasks, and attempts. Name the Spark version, AQE setting, and input layout alongside the numbers.

Two claims fail often. “One action is one job”: false here for reads, broadcasts, show(), and anything with a shuffle under AQE. “A second action reuses the earlier shuffle”: without a cache, show() and a later write on the same aggregate each ran their own shuffle, and neither skipped a stage from the other. Skipped stages showed up between jobs started for the same action. The exception was a cached aggregate, where the later write skipped the map stage.

question: An interviewer asks how many jobs df.groupBy("k").count().show() creates. How do you answer?
answer: I would not give one number without conditions. The plan has one hash shuffle, so with AQE off the first job has two stages: scan tasks, one per input partition, then post-shuffle tasks. show() needs 21 rows and scans the 200 shuffle partitions in rounds, and each round is another job that lists the map stage as skipped. How many rounds depends on where the keys land. With AQE on, the shuffle stage runs as its own job and AQE usually coalesces small output, so a second job often finishes it. A read that infers a schema adds jobs before any of this. Then I would verify with job groups and the Jobs tab.

title: The PySpark coding round: six patterns
dek: Six problems that recur in 30–45 minute data engineering coding rounds — each solved, run, and costed, with the wrong answer that looks right.
idea: Most coding-round problems are a window, an aggregation, or a generator applied to a precisely stated grain. Say the grain, the tie rule, the null rule, and the time boundary before you code, then name the operator that shuffles.

sections.title: How to work the round
sections.body:
In a 30–45 minute round the code is the last third of the work. Before typing, pin down the contract out loud:

  • Grain and keys — one output row per what, and which columns identify a record?
  • Ordering and ties — “latest” by which column, and what breaks a tie when two rows share it?
  • Nulls — null keys, null timestamps, null or empty arrays: dropped, kept, or sorted last?
  • Time — event time or ingest time, which time zone, and are boundaries inclusive? Is a gap of exactly 30 minutes a new session?

Then build a five-to-eight-row input with spark.createDataFrame that contains each edge case, say the expected output before you run it, and only then write the transformation. Finish with the cost: which operator shuffles (an Exchange in explain()), what is sorted, and whether anything collapses into a single partition.

Every block below was run exactly as shown on local PySpark 3.5.7 (local[2], JDK 17) with an existing spark session, spark.sql.session.timeZone set to UTC, and spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to 4; the SCD block adds Delta Lake 3.2.1, and one demonstration also ran on a two-executor local cluster. Outputs are copied from those runs. Plans quoted in prose come from the same runtime with adaptive query execution (AQE) at its default, enabled, unless stated.

Check the sources: Window functions reference

sections.title: 1. Deduplicate, keeping the latest row per key
sections.body:
Problem. A customer feed repeats customer_id. Keep one row per customer: the newest by updated_at; when two rows share a timestamp, the higher ingest_id wins; a null timestamp loses to any real one. The tiny input contains all three cases.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

customers = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, "a@old.example", "2026-09-01 09:00:00", 101),
    (1, "a@new.example", "2026-09-03 18:30:00", 102),
    (2, "b@one.example", "2026-09-02 12:00:00", 201),
    (2, "b@two.example", "2026-09-02 12:00:00", 202),  # same timestamp: a tie
    (3, "c@only.example", None, 301),                 # null timestamp
], "customer_id int, email string, updated_at string, ingest_id int"
).withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at"))

latest_first = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(
    F.col("updated_at").desc_nulls_last(), F.col("ingest_id").desc())

latest = (customers
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(latest_first))
    .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn"))
latest.orderBy("customer_id").show(truncate=False)

# Same answer without a window: max over a struct compares fields left to right
by_struct = (customers
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .agg(F.max(F.struct("updated_at", "ingest_id", "email")).alias("r"))
    .select("customer_id", "r.email", "r.updated_at", "r.ingest_id"))
by_struct.orderBy("customer_id").show(truncate=False)
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+
|customer_id|email         |updated_at         |ingest_id|
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+
|1          |a@new.example |2026-09-03 18:30:00|102      |
|2          |b@two.example |2026-09-02 12:00:00|202      |
|3          |c@only.example|NULL               |301      |
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+

+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+
|customer_id|email         |updated_at         |ingest_id|
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+
|1          |a@new.example |2026-09-03 18:30:00|102      |
|2          |b@two.example |2026-09-02 12:00:00|202      |
|3          |c@only.example|NULL               |301      |
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+---------+

Cost. The window is one hash shuffle on customer_id and a sort inside each partition. In Spark 3.5.7 the optimizer recognizes the rn == 1 filter and inserts WindowGroupLimit twice — Partial below the Exchange and Final above it (observed in explain() on an equivalent query) — so each task forwards only its local winners. The struct version is an aggregation: max over a struct compares fields left to right, so the field order is the tie rule, and in a separate check a struct whose first field was null lost to one with a real timestamp. Its plan was a SortAggregate with a partial max before the shuffle. max_by(col, ord), available since 3.3, is the one-column shortcut; its documentation says nothing about ties on ord, so pass a struct as ord when ties can happen.

The common wrong answer is df.orderBy(F.col("ts").desc()).dropDuplicates(["key"]). For a batch DataFrame the API documentation says only that it drops duplicate rows, not which one survives. In the 3.5.7 optimizer, ReplaceDeduplicateWithAggregate turns deduplication into an aggregate that keeps First of every non-key column. The observed plan is the global sort, a partial_first in each task, a hash Exchange on the key, and a final first: the winner depends on the order in which the final aggregate reads shuffle output, and the earlier sort does not control that. The block below makes it visible. It disables AQE itself, and its timestamps are unique, so no tie excuses the result.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
events = (spark.range(0, 200000, 1, 8)
    .withColumn("key", F.col("id") % 40000)
    .withColumn("ts", (F.col("id") * 7919) % 1000003))  # timestamps are unique

expected = (events
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("key").orderBy(F.col("ts").desc())))
    .filter("rn = 1")
    .select("key", F.col("id").alias("expected_id")))

risky = events.orderBy(F.col("ts").desc()).dropDuplicates(["key"])

wrong = risky.join(expected, "key").filter("id <> expected_id").count()
print("keys:", expected.count(), "| dropDuplicates kept a non-latest row for:", wrong)
  • local[2]: keys: 40000 | dropDuplicates kept a non-latest row for: 0
  • local-cluster[2,1,1024], run 1: keys: 40000 | dropDuplicates kept a non-latest row for: 29351
  • local-cluster[2,1,1024], run 2: keys: 40000 | dropDuplicates kept a non-latest row for: 19926

The single-process run matched on every key, which is how this bug survives a unit test. With AQE left on, two runs of a close variant on the same two-executor cluster also matched; that is an observation, not a guarantee the API makes.

sections.title: 2. Sessionize events with a 30-minute inactivity gap
sections.body:
Problem. Give each event a session ID: a session starts at a user's first event or after more than 30 minutes without one. Decide the boundary aloud. Here a gap of exactly 30 minutes stays in the session (events 2 and 3), and a 40-minute gap splits it (events 3 and 4).

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

events = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("u1", 1, "2026-09-01 10:00:00"),
    ("u1", 2, "2026-09-01 10:20:00"),
    ("u1", 3, "2026-09-01 10:50:00"),  # exactly 30 minutes later: same session
    ("u1", 4, "2026-09-01 11:30:00"),  # 40 minutes later: new session
    ("u2", 5, "2026-09-01 10:05:00"),
    ("u2", 6, "2026-09-01 12:00:00"),
], "user_id string, event_id int, ts string").withColumn("ts", F.to_timestamp("ts"))

by_user = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("ts", "event_id")
gap_seconds = F.col("ts").cast("long") - F.lag("ts").over(by_user).cast("long")

sessions = (events
    .withColumn("new_session", F.when(gap_seconds.isNull() | (gap_seconds > 30 * 60), 1).otherwise(0))
    .withColumn("session_no", F.sum("new_session").over(
        by_user.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)))
    .withColumn("session_id", F.concat_ws("-", "user_id", F.col("session_no").cast("string"))))
sessions.select("user_id", "event_id", "ts", "new_session", "session_id").orderBy("event_id").show()

# Built-in alternative (3.2+): one row per session, end = last event + gap
(events
    .groupBy("user_id", F.session_window("ts", "30 minutes").alias("s"))
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("events"))
    .select("user_id", "s.start", "s.end", "events")
    .orderBy("user_id", "start")
    .show())
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7
+-------+--------+-------------------+-----------+----------+
|user_id|event_id|                 ts|new_session|session_id|
+-------+--------+-------------------+-----------+----------+
|     u1|       1|2026-09-01 10:00:00|          1|      u1-1|
|     u1|       2|2026-09-01 10:20:00|          0|      u1-1|
|     u1|       3|2026-09-01 10:50:00|          0|      u1-1|
|     u1|       4|2026-09-01 11:30:00|          1|      u1-2|
|     u2|       5|2026-09-01 10:05:00|          1|      u2-1|
|     u2|       6|2026-09-01 12:00:00|          1|      u2-2|
+-------+--------+-------------------+-----------+----------+

+-------+-------------------+-------------------+------+
|user_id|              start|                end|events|
+-------+-------------------+-------------------+------+
|     u1|2026-09-01 10:00:00|2026-09-01 11:20:00|     3|
|     u1|2026-09-01 11:30:00|2026-09-01 12:00:00|     1|
|     u2|2026-09-01 10:05:00|2026-09-01 10:35:00|     1|
|     u2|2026-09-01 12:00:00|2026-09-01 12:30:00|     1|
+-------+-------------------+-------------------+------+

How it works and what it costs. lag reads the previous timestamp within the user; the flag is 1 at a first event or after a gap over 1,800 seconds; a running sum of flags numbers the sessions. Both window functions share one specification, so the plan is a single hash Exchange on the user, one sort, and one Window operator. A very active user still lands in one task: sessionization inherits key skew. The frame is explicit on purpose. With an ordering and no frame, PySpark uses a range frame from unbounded preceding to the current row, which includes every row with an equal ordering value; event_id in the ordering and a rows frame keep the numbering deterministic when timestamps collide.

The built-in alternative. session_window(ts, "30 minutes") (3.2+) groups events into sessions that end at the latest event plus the gap: the observed first session ends at 11:20, which is 10:50 plus 30 minutes. On this input it agreed with the window version, including the exactly-30-minute gap. It returns one row per session rather than labeling events, and the gap can be a column expression evaluated per row. In Structured Streaming, the guide's example pairs it with a watermark; Update output mode is not supported, and the grouping key needs at least one column besides the session window (batch queries may group by the session window alone). The lag version cannot run on a stream: starting it failed with NON_TIME_WINDOW_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_STREAMING.

The common wrong answer is a fixed time bucket. Buckets cut on the clock, not on inactivity: a 30-minute tumbling window splits clicks at 10:29 and 10:31 into two sessions, and an hourly groupBy merges visits at 10:00 and 10:50 that were 50 minutes apart. The other frequent slip is stopping at the gap flag, which marks where sessions start but gives the rows in between no ID until you take the running sum.

sections.title: 3. A running 7-day active user count
sections.body:
Problem. For every date, count the distinct users with any activity on that date or the six days before it. The input has gaps (nothing on 09-03, 09-04, or 09-06 to 09-08) and a user active on consecutive days, because those are exactly what break the easy answers.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

activity = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("u1", "2026-09-01"), ("u2", "2026-09-01"), ("u1", "2026-09-02"),
    ("u3", "2026-09-05"), ("u1", "2026-09-09"),
    ("u1", "2026-09-10"), ("u2", "2026-09-10"), ("u4", "2026-09-10"),
], "user_id string, d string").withColumn("d", F.to_date("d"))

try:
    activity.withColumn("n", F.countDistinct("user_id").over(Window.orderBy("d").rowsBetween(-6, 0)))
except Exception as e:
    print(str(e).split(";")[0])

# Correct: credit each active user-day to the 7 as-of dates whose window contains it
user_days = activity.select("user_id", "d").distinct()
credited = user_days.withColumn("as_of", F.explode(F.sequence("d", F.date_add("d", 6))))
active = credited.groupBy("as_of").agg(F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("active_7d"))
spine = (activity.agg(F.min("d").alias("lo"), F.max("d").alias("hi"))
    .select(F.explode(F.sequence("lo", "hi")).alias("as_of")))
correct = spine.join(active, "as_of", "left").fillna(0, ["active_7d"])

# Wrong: sum daily distinct counts over 7 rows, or over a 7-day range
by_day = Window.orderBy("day_no")
daily = (activity.groupBy("d").agg(F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("dau"))
    .withColumn("day_no", F.datediff("d", F.lit("1970-01-01")))
    .withColumn("rows_sum", F.sum("dau").over(by_day.rowsBetween(-6, 0)))
    .withColumn("range_sum", F.sum("dau").over(by_day.rangeBetween(-6, 0))))

(correct
    .join(daily.select(F.col("d").alias("as_of"), "dau", "rows_sum", "range_sum"), "as_of", "left")
    .orderBy("as_of")
    .show())

# Also correct, on active days only: a set over a 7-day range frame (one global partition)
(user_days
    .withColumn("day_no", F.datediff("d", F.lit("1970-01-01")))
    .withColumn("active_7d", F.size(F.collect_set("user_id").over(by_day.rangeBetween(-6, 0))))
    .select("d", "active_7d").distinct()
    .orderBy("d")
    .show())
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7
[DISTINCT_WINDOW_FUNCTION_UNSUPPORTED] Distinct window functions are not supported: "count(DISTINCT user_id) OVER (ORDER BY d ASC NULLS FIRST ROWS BETWEEN -6 FOLLOWING AND CURRENT ROW)".
+----------+---------+----+--------+---------+
|     as_of|active_7d| dau|rows_sum|range_sum|
+----------+---------+----+--------+---------+
|2026-09-01|        2|   2|       2|        2|
|2026-09-02|        2|   1|       3|        3|
|2026-09-03|        2|NULL|    NULL|     NULL|
|2026-09-04|        2|NULL|    NULL|     NULL|
|2026-09-05|        3|   1|       4|        4|
|2026-09-06|        3|NULL|    NULL|     NULL|
|2026-09-07|        3|NULL|    NULL|     NULL|
|2026-09-08|        2|NULL|    NULL|     NULL|
|2026-09-09|        2|   1|       5|        2|
|2026-09-10|        4|   3|       8|        5|
+----------+---------+----+--------+---------+

+----------+---------+
|         d|active_7d|
+----------+---------+
|2026-09-01|        2|
|2026-09-02|        2|
|2026-09-05|        3|
|2026-09-09|        2|
|2026-09-10|        4|
+----------+---------+

Reading the result. The first line is the exact error Spark 3.5.7 raises for a distinct count over a window frame: the literal translation of the requirement does not analyze. active_7d is correct. rows_sum adds the last seven rows of daily counts; with gaps those rows reach back more than seven days, so 09-09 reports 5 against a true 2. range_sum uses rangeBetween(-6, 0) on a day number, which fixes the calendar but still adds per-day distinct counts: u1 on 09-09 and 09-10 is counted twice, giving 5 against 4 (and 3 against 2 on 09-02). A range frame with an offset needs a single numeric ordering expression, which is why the date becomes day_no.

Cost. The explode approach deduplicates user-days, multiplies them by seven, and groups by as_of. For the distinct count the plan has two aggregation shuffles — one on (as_of, user_id), then one on as_of — and no global sort, so it spreads across executors. The spine join adds dates without events, drops the six trailing dates the explode creates past the last day, and turns an empty week into 0. The collect_set version is correct on active days, but a window with no partitionBy moves every row into one partition: the run logged No Partition Defined for Window operation! Moving all data to a single partition, this can cause serious performance degradation. Each row also carries that week's set of users. Use it only for small inputs, or partition it by a column such as tenant.

The common wrong answer is either sum above, or a countDistinct over a window that Spark refuses. State the definition first: daily active users do not add up to weekly active users.

sections.title: 4. SCD Type 2 with a Delta MERGE
sections.body:
Problem. Maintain dim_customer with valid_from, valid_to, and is_current. Each batch carries (customer_id, city, effective_date). An unchanged row does nothing; a changed city closes the current version and inserts a new one; a new key inserts a current row. The block assumes a session with Delta Lake 3.2.1's SQL extension and catalog configured.

The trick. A changed key needs two actions in one MERGE — an update and an insert — but each source row either matches or it does not. So the source is staged as a union: every batch row keyed by merge_key = customer_id, which matches the current version and closes it if the city changed, plus an extra copy of each changed row with a NULL merge_key. NULL never equals anything, so that copy falls through to whenNotMatchedInsert and becomes the new version. A new key has no current row, so its keyed copy is inserted.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
import tempfile
from datetime import date
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

path = tempfile.mkdtemp() + "/dim_customer"
(spark.createDataFrame([], "customer_id int, city string, valid_from date, valid_to date, is_current boolean")
    .write.format("delta").save(path))

def apply_scd2(updates):
    dim = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path)
    current = dim.toDF().filter("is_current")
    # Changed keys need a second row: a NULL merge_key never matches, so it is inserted
    new_versions = (updates.alias("u")
        .join(current.alias("c"), F.col("u.customer_id") == F.col("c.customer_id"))
        .filter(~F.col("u.city").eqNullSafe(F.col("c.city")))
        .select(F.lit(None).cast("int").alias("merge_key"), "u.*"))
    staged = new_versions.unionByName(
        updates.select(F.col("customer_id").alias("merge_key"), "*"))
    (dim.alias("t")
        .merge(staged.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current")
        .whenMatchedUpdate(
            condition="NOT (t.city <=> s.city)",
            set={"is_current": "false", "valid_to": "s.effective_date"})
        .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
            "customer_id": "s.customer_id", "city": "s.city",
            "valid_from": "s.effective_date", "valid_to": "null", "is_current": "true"})
        .execute())

batch = "customer_id int, city string, effective_date date"
load_1 = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Austin", date(2026, 9, 1)), (2, "Denver", date(2026, 9, 1))], batch)
load_2 = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, "Austin", date(2026, 9, 10)),   # unchanged
    (2, "Boston", date(2026, 9, 10)),   # changed attribute
    (3, "Chicago", date(2026, 9, 10)),  # new key
], batch)

apply_scd2(load_1)
apply_scd2(load_2)
spark.read.format("delta").load(path).orderBy("customer_id", "valid_from").show()

apply_scd2(load_2)  # replaying the same batch
m = F.col("operationMetrics")
(DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).history()
    .select("version", "operation",
            m["numTargetRowsInserted"].alias("inserted"), m["numTargetRowsUpdated"].alias("updated"))
    .orderBy("version")
    .show())
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7 · DELTA LAKE 3.2.1
+-----------+-------+----------+----------+----------+
|customer_id|   city|valid_from|  valid_to|is_current|
+-----------+-------+----------+----------+----------+
|          1| Austin|2026-09-01|      NULL|      true|
|          2| Denver|2026-09-01|2026-09-10|     false|
|          2| Boston|2026-09-10|      NULL|      true|
|          3|Chicago|2026-09-10|      NULL|      true|
+-----------+-------+----------+----------+----------+

+-------+---------+--------+-------+
|version|operation|inserted|updated|
+-------+---------+--------+-------+
|      0|    WRITE|    NULL|   NULL|
|      1|    MERGE|       2|      0|
|      2|    MERGE|       2|      1|
|      3|    MERGE|       0|      0|
+-------+---------+--------+-------+

Reading the result. After two loads, customer 2 has a closed Denver row ending 2026-09-10 and a current Boston row; customer 1 is untouched; customer 3 is new. The history shows the second MERGE inserted 2 rows and updated 1, and replaying the same batch inserted and updated nothing, because unchanged rows match but fail the update condition. Each load is one table version, so a reader never sees a closed row without its replacement.

Details that separate a senior answer. Compare with <=> (eqNullSafe), not <>: the Delta documentation's SCD example uses <>, which is never true when either side is null, so a change to or from null would be missed. Put t.is_current in the match condition so closed history rows never match. Deduplicate the batch to one row per key first (problem 1): a separate run with two source rows for one target row failed with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. Replay is safe only for the same batch; a late batch with an older effective_date would close the current row with an earlier date, so apply batches in order or add a date guard to the conditions. Cost: the staging join against current rows is a shuffle, or a broadcast when the batch is small, and by default MERGE searches the entire target table for matches; the Delta documentation's tuning advice is to add known constraints, such as partition predicates, to the match condition.

The common wrong answer is a MERGE on customer_id alone with an update clause and an insert clause: a changed key matches, is closed, and its new version is never inserted, because a matched source row cannot also take the not-matched branch. The other is an UPDATE followed by a separate INSERT — two commits, with a moment in which the key has no current row, and a failure between them leaves it that way.

Check the sources: Delta Lake 3.2.1: merge and SCD Type 2

sections.title: 5. Top N per group
sections.body:
Problem. Return the top two reps by amount in each region. East has a tie at 90, so state the tie rule before choosing a function.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

sales = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("east", "ann", 90), ("east", "bo", 90), ("east", "cy", 80), ("east", "di", 70),
    ("west", "ed", 95), ("west", "fay", 60),
], "region string, rep string, amount int")

by_amount = Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(F.col("amount").desc())
by_amount_then_rep = Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(F.col("amount").desc(), "rep")

(sales.select("*",
        F.row_number().over(by_amount_then_rep).alias("row_number"),
        F.rank().over(by_amount).alias("rank"),
        F.dense_rank().over(by_amount).alias("dense_rank"))
    .orderBy("region", "row_number")
    .show())

top2 = (sales
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(by_amount_then_rep))
    .filter(F.col("rn") <= 2))
top2.orderBy("region", "rn").show()

print(sales.orderBy(F.col("amount").desc(), "rep").limit(2).collect())

top2.explain()
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7
+------+---+------+----------+----+----------+
|region|rep|amount|row_number|rank|dense_rank|
+------+---+------+----------+----+----------+
|  east|ann|    90|         1|   1|         1|
|  east| bo|    90|         2|   1|         1|
|  east| cy|    80|         3|   3|         2|
|  east| di|    70|         4|   4|         3|
|  west| ed|    95|         1|   1|         1|
|  west|fay|    60|         2|   2|         2|
+------+---+------+----------+----+----------+

+------+---+------+---+
|region|rep|amount| rn|
+------+---+------+---+
|  east|ann|    90|  1|
|  east| bo|    90|  2|
|  west| ed|    95|  1|
|  west|fay|    60|  2|
+------+---+------+---+

[Row(region='west', rep='ed', amount=95), Row(region='east', rep='ann', amount=90)]
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- Filter (rn#58 <= 2)
   +- Window [row_number() windowspecdefinition(region#0, amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST, specifiedwindowframe(RowFrame, unboundedpreceding$(), currentrow$())) AS rn#58], [region#0], [amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST]
      +- WindowGroupLimit [region#0], [amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST], row_number(), 2, Final
         +- Sort [region#0 ASC NULLS FIRST, amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
            +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#0, 4), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=177]
               +- WindowGroupLimit [region#0], [amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST], row_number(), 2, Partial
                  +- Sort [region#0 ASC NULLS FIRST, amount#2 DESC NULLS LAST, rep#1 ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
                     +- Scan ExistingRDD[region#0,rep#1,amount#2]

Choosing the ranking function. row_number gives exactly N rows per group, but which tied row wins is arbitrary unless the ordering includes a tie-breaker (rep here). rank gives ties the same number and skips the next (1, 1, 3), so rank <= 2 would return ann and bo for east. dense_rank does not skip (1, 1, 2), so dense_rank <= 2 would return ann, bo, and cy — more than N rows. Pick by the business rule: exactly N, every row tied at the cutoff, or the top N distinct values.

Cost. The plan above is one hash Exchange on region with a sort on each side. Spark 3.5.7's InferWindowGroupLimit rule recognized rn <= 2 and inserted WindowGroupLimit as Partial before the shuffle and Final after it, so tasks forward at most two rows per region instead of every row. The rule covers rank-like functions filtered by limit-like predicates and is controlled by the internal setting spark.sql.optimizer.windowGroupLimitThreshold (default 1000).

The common wrong answer is sales.orderBy(F.col("amount").desc()).limit(2). It returns the top two rows of the whole DataFrame — the printed rows are west's ed and east's ann, and every other row in east is gone. Cost is not the problem: in a separate check, orderBy(...).limit(2) planned as TakeOrderedAndProject(limit=2, ...), a top-N selection rather than a full global sort. Looping over regions with a filter and limit for each is correct but runs one query per group.

sections.title: 6. Flatten nested JSON and arrays of structs
sections.body:
Problem. Orders arrive as JSON with a nested customer struct and an items array of structs. Produce one row per item with the customer fields, keeping orders whose array is empty or missing.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

lines = [
    '{"order_id": 1, "customer": {"id": "c1", "address": {"city": "Austin"}},'
    ' "items": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "B", "qty": 1}]}',
    '{"order_id": 2, "customer": {"id": "c2", "address": null}, "items": []}',
    '{"order_id": 3, "customer": {"id": "c3"}}',
]
schema = ("order_id INT, customer STRUCT<id: STRING, address: STRUCT<city: STRING>>, "
          "items ARRAY<STRUCT<sku: STRING, qty: INT>>")

# Schema first: no inference pass; in production this is .json("s3://.../orders/")
orders = spark.read.schema(schema).json(spark.sparkContext.parallelize(lines))

flat = (orders
    .select("order_id",
            F.col("customer.id").alias("customer_id"),
            F.col("customer.address.city").alias("city"),
            F.posexplode_outer("items").alias("pos", "item"))
    .select("order_id", "customer_id", "city", "pos", "item.*"))
flat.orderBy("order_id", "pos").show()

print("explode rows:", orders.select(F.explode("items")).count(),
      "| explode_outer rows:", orders.select(F.explode_outer("items")).count())
orders.select("order_id", F.inline_outer("items")).orderBy("order_id").show()
orders.select("order_id", "customer.*").orderBy("order_id").show()
OBSERVED OUTPUT · LOCAL PYSPARK 3.5.7
+--------+-----------+------+----+----+----+
|order_id|customer_id|  city| pos| sku| qty|
+--------+-----------+------+----+----+----+
|       1|         c1|Austin|   0|   A|   2|
|       1|         c1|Austin|   1|   B|   1|
|       2|         c2|  NULL|NULL|NULL|NULL|
|       3|         c3|  NULL|NULL|NULL|NULL|
+--------+-----------+------+----+----+----+

explode rows: 2 | explode_outer rows: 4
+--------+----+----+
|order_id| sku| qty|
+--------+----+----+
|       1|   A|   2|
|       1|   B|   1|
|       2|NULL|NULL|
|       3|NULL|NULL|
+--------+----+----+

+--------+---+--------+
|order_id| id| address|
+--------+---+--------+
|       1| c1|{Austin}|
|       2| c2|    NULL|
|       3| c3|    NULL|
+--------+---+--------+

How it works. The DDL string fixes the schema, so Spark does not run an inference pass over the input (by default inference uses every input object: samplingRatio is 1.0), and a missing field becomes null rather than changing the schema. Dotted paths reach into structs: customer.address.city is null when address is null (order 2) or absent (order 3), and customer.* expands one level. explode produced 2 rows because it drops parents whose array is empty or null; explode_outer produced 4. posexplode_outer adds the element position, useful for keeping item order or deduplicating line items, and inline_outer turns an array of structs straight into columns. For malformed input, the default PERMISSIVE mode sets unparsable fields to null and keeps the raw record only if the schema includes the string column named by columnNameOfCorruptRecord.

Cost. Generators are narrow: an explode_outer plan in a separate check was a single Generate operator with no Exchange. The cost is row multiplication. Exploding two independent arrays one after the other yields their cross product, so explode one array per output table, or zip related arrays with arrays_zip and explode once.

The common wrong answer is plain explode on an optional array, which silently removes orders 2 and 3, often combined with schema inference on every run, so that one unusual file can change column types downstream.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

customers = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, "a@old.example", "2026-09-01 09:00:00", 101),
    (1, "a@new.example", "2026-09-03 18:30:00", 102),
    (2, "b@one.example", "2026-09-02 12:00:00", 201),
    (2, "b@two.example", "2026-09-02 12:00:00", 202),  # same timestamp: a tie
    (3, "c@only.example", None, 301),                 # null timestamp
], "customer_id int, email string, updated_at string, ingest_id int"
).withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at"))

latest_first = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(
    F.col("updated_at").desc_nulls_last(), F.col("ingest_id").desc())

latest = (customers
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(latest_first))
    .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn"))
latest.orderBy("customer_id").show(truncate=False)

# Same answer without a window: max over a struct compares fields left to right
by_struct = (customers
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .agg(F.max(F.struct("updated_at", "ingest_id", "email")).alias("r"))
    .select("customer_id", "r.email", "r.updated_at", "r.ingest_id"))
by_struct.orderBy("customer_id").show(truncate=False)
output: Both tables printed the same three rows: customer 1 kept a@new.example (2026-09-03 18:30:00, ingest_id 102); customer 2 kept b@two.example, the 2026-09-02 12:00:00 tie broken by the higher ingest_id 202; customer 3 kept c@only.example with a NULL updated_at, its only row. The tie-breaker is what makes the result deterministic; without it, customer 2's survivor is arbitrary.
runtime: Ran on local PySpark 3.5.7 (local[2], JDK 17) on 2026-09-15; output above is observed. The lesson's other blocks ran on the same runtime; the SCD block also used Delta Lake 3.2.1, and the dropDuplicates demonstration also ran on a two-executor local-cluster master.
pitfall: Trusting a test that passed in local mode. orderBy followed by dropDuplicates returned the latest row for every key in local[2], and a non-latest row for tens of thousands of keys on a two-executor local cluster with AQE disabled. Put the tie, the null, and the gap into the tiny input, and prefer operators whose result is defined by the query rather than by the order in which tasks and shuffle blocks happen to run.
question: Your deduplication used orderBy(...).dropDuplicates([key]) and its unit test passed. Why can it still keep the wrong row, and what do you write instead?
answer: dropDuplicates promises that duplicates are removed, not which row survives. Spark 3.5.7 rewrites it into an aggregate that takes first() of every non-key column; that aggregate runs partially in each task, shuffles by key, and combines partial results in the order the shuffle output is read, so the preceding sort does not pick the winner. A single-process test can pass by accident: in local[2] every key matched, while a two-executor local cluster with AQE disabled kept a non-latest row for 29,351 and then 19,926 of 40,000 keys. Write row_number over a window partitioned by the key and ordered by timestamp descending plus a unique tie-breaker, and keep row 1, or take max over a struct whose field order encodes the same rule.
